articles.title: Trump administration asks Washington to set aside ballots from 400 voters it says may be noncitizens
articles.summary: SEATTLE (AP) — The Trump administration on Monday asked Washington state to set aside any ballots received from more than 400 people it alleges registered to...
articles.body:
SEATTLE (AP) — The Trump administration on Monday asked Washington state to set aside any ballots received from more than 400 people it alleges registered to vote without U.S. citizenship, less than two weeks after making a similar demand in California.

The announcement is the latest sign of the administration's attempts to sow doubts about the election or its outcome in states with races that will help determine control of the U.S. Senate and House.

In a letter to Washington Secretary of State Steve Hobbs, the Justice Department said it had identified 1,500 votes cast by the more than 400 people in prior elections. It asked the state to set aside any ballots they might cast in next month's midterm until state officials can confirm they are legally eligible to vote. The state has more than 5 million registered voters, and the state issues mail ballots to all of them.

One listed voter last cast a ballot in 1994

At a news conference, Neil Floyd, the acting U.S. attorney in Seattle, said he believed the 405 voters identified so far represented "the tip of the iceberg."

"Because of limitations the state has placed on our investigation, we've only been able to uncover a fraction of the total number," he said.

Hobbs said he was reviewing the DOJ's request. His office noted that the data shared by the department included the last time each of the 405 people voted. One was in 1994.

"The timing of this request — one week before the General Election — is no doubt intended to cast unfounded suspicion on the results," Hobbs said.

Much of the list was built based on "recent contacts" with suspected noncitizens, Floyd said, because federal officers are now routinely checking to see if the people they interact with are registered to vote.

Lack of state cooperation a problem, DOJ says

Without access to those state records, proving someone illegally voted will be difficult, Floyd said. The Justice Department has demanded information including addresses, dates of birth, driver's license numbers and partial Social Security numbers.

The effort is the latest by the administration to identify noncitizen voters , even though noncitizen voting is exceptionally rare. President Donald Trump has repeatedly sought to undermine public confidence in elections.

Meanwhile, Washington officials have noted that changes in U.S. Postal Service operations have disenfranchised thousands of legitimate voters.

The Washington request marks the third time this month that the Justice Department has brought a direct state challenge as voting is underway. All three states — Washington, California and Alaska — have House or Senate races that will help determine the balance of power in the nation's Capitol.

The race for Washington's 3rd Congressional District is one of the most competitive in the country in this year's midterm elections. Democrats are counting on Rep. Maria Gluesenkamp Perez winning reelection as crucial to their strategy of retaking the majority in the U.S. House. She has won twice in a district that also has supported Trump each time he's been on the ballot.

The Justice Department sued in California as part of a similar attempt to require the state to set aside mail ballots from up to 20,000 people the federal government suspects may not be citizens. Another lawsuit filed in Alaska last week seeks to delay certification of the vote if the Republican incumbent doesn't win.

In California, a panel of federal appellate judges heard rare Sunday arguments and questioned the timing, constitutionality and authority of the Justice Department's demand. On Monday, they declined to rule on the expedited timeline the DOJ requested and sent it back to a lower court.

The Elections Clause of the U.S. Constitution gives state legislatures the power to set the time, place and manner of congressional elections.

Los Angeles County Assistant Registrar-Recorder Monica Flores said in a court filing that her staff went through a sample of 200 records from the Trump administration's list. They found the sample included canceled or inactive registrations, people with no voting history and voters who appeared to have been born in the United States.

The Justice Department told Washington it anticipates sending the state an additional list of people it suspects are not citizens prior to Election Day. It also noted that some of the people it suspects registered without citizenship may have since become naturalized.

Investigations into prior allegations of noncitizen voters have revealed far fewer instances than the Trump administration has claimed. In Nevada, Trump's administration alleged there were 1,500 potential noncitizen voters on the rolls but subsequent investigation found zero.

In Maricopa County, which includes Phoenix, the county recorder, who is a Trump supporter, announced that there were 207 possible noncitizens on the county's rolls. The Republican County Attorney determined there were actually eight. ___ Boone reported from Boise, Idaho.

articles.title: What are the investigations into Flávio Bolsonaro, who fled Brazil? | G1
articles.standfirst: For readers outside Brazil, g1 explains the Supreme Court investigations into the son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, his runoff defeat to Lula and his decision to flee to the US.
articles.summary: g1 explains the Supreme Court investigations into the son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, his runoff defeat to Lula and his fraud claims, made without evidence.
articles.body:
Flávio Bolsonaro — Foto: Adriano Machado/Reuters

Brazilian Senator Flávio Bolsonaro fled the country after losing the presidential election to Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva on Sunday (October 25) and declaring that he would not recognize the results. The defeated candidate arrived in the United States on Wednesday morning (October 28).

In Brazil, Flávio is under investigation in two cases before the Supreme Federal Court ( STF ) , Brazil's highest court. The investigations involve suspected irregularities in the financing of a film about his father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, and alleged money laundering involving an online betting business and financial transactions linked to Willer Tomaz, a lawyer and friend of Flávio.

For readers outside Brazil, g1 explains in English the Supreme Court investigations into the son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, his runoff defeat to Lula and his fraud claims, made without evidence.

Who is Flávio Bolsonaro? The eldest son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, the 45-year-old senator represents the state of Rio de Janeiro. He is married and holds a law degree. He began his political career at age 21 and served four terms as a state legislator before being elected to the Brazilian Senate in 2018 with more than 4 million votes.

Chosen by his father in December 2025 to represent Bolsonarism, the right-wing political movement associated with Jair Bolsonaro, in the 2026 presidential election, he was defeated in the runoff.

One investigation is looking into Flávio's possible involvement in crimes related to the financing of Dark Horse , an unreleased biographical film about his father, former President Jair Bolsonaro.

The case came to light less than six months after Flávio announced his intention to run for president, following a report by the news outlet The Intercept Brasil. The outlet published audio recordings and messages showing that Flávio asked for a payment of R$ 130 million (US$ 24 million) to Daniel Vorcaro, the former banker behind Banco Master, to finance Dark Horse.

g1 and TV Globo obtained documents showing that Vorcaro paid R$61 million (US$ 11 million).

Who is Daniel Vorcaro? Vorcaro is a Brazilian businessman who owned Banco Master, a bank ordered into liquidation by Brazil's Central Bank in 2025. He was arrested by the Federal Police (PF), Brazil's national law enforcement agency, in November of that year on suspicion of financial fraud and arrested again in March 2026 as part of a sweeping investigation into alleged corruption, money laundering and intimidation.

"Brother, I thought I'd send you this voice message so you could listen to it carefully. [...] I know you're going through an extremely difficult time too, with all this confusion, not knowing exactly how things are going to turn out. And even though you told us we could ask you for the money, Daniel, I feel uncomfortable constantly chasing you for it, OK?" Flávio said in one of the conversations.

The case was marked by several contradictions in Flávio's statements about his relationship with Vorcaro. On the day the story broke, Flávio denied that Vorcaro had financed the film and dismissed questions from The Intercept Brasil’s reporter as "political activism."

Hours later, the then-presidential hopeful released a video confirming that he had requested money from Vorcaro but denying any wrongdoing. He also said he had no "improper ties" to the banker and called for a parliamentary inquiry into Banco Master in Brazil's Congress.

In an interview with GloboNews in May, Flávio explained that he had initially denied the banker's involvement in the film because of confidentiality agreements.

"I didn't say it was a lie. I have a confidentiality agreement. I'm talking about it now because it has come to light. There's no way to deny it anymore," he said.

In the same interview, Flávio said payments totaling R$61 million (US$ 11 million) had been made by May 2025. In September, however, Brazilian magazine Piauí reported that Vorcaro had made another payment of US$1.6 million, bringing the total to approximately R$70 million (US$ 12 million).

Flávio said his relationship with Vorcaro was limited to the film and that there would be "no surprises." Four days later, however, following new revelations from the brazilian press, the senator acknowledged visiting Vorcaro after the banker's first arrest, while Vorcaro was under house arrest and wearing an electronic ankle monitor, to end negotiations over the film.

"Yes, I went to meet him to put an end to this story, to say that if he had told me how serious the situation was, I would have looked for another investor much earlier, and the film wouldn't have been at risk," he said.

Another contradiction concerned the film's financial records. On May 19, Flávio said he had instructed the production company to provide a detailed accounting of how the money was spent within 30 days.

The deadline passed on June 18 without either the candidate or the production company making the promised documents public.

When questioned, Flávio cited a report from a private expert examination, submitted by the film's producer, Karina Gama, as part of an investigation by the Civil Police of São Paulo, a state-level law enforcement agency.

The report, commissioned by the producer herself, said the film's expenses totaled R$75 million (US$ 14 million) but did not include receipts or invoices supporting those expenses.

Another contradiction in Flávio's statements about Banco Master emerged when the senator denied being close to Vorcaro after former First Lady Michelle Bolsonaro shared a social media post about alleged parties hosted by the banker.

"I want to assure you: the only relationship I have with Vorcaro is about my father's film. That's it. You won't see me at Vorcaro's parties. I've never been on Vorcaro's plane, and I've never been to any astronaut-themed party," he said at a gathering with female supporters.

His statement about the plane resurfaced after Piauí reported that, on January 19, 2025, Flávio, his wife and their two daughters flew from Fort Lauderdale, in the United States, to Brasília, Brazil's capital, aboard a Legacy 650 aircraft aby Prime You, a company in which Vorcaro was a partner at the time.

The aircraft was jointly owned. One ownership stake was linked to Prime You, while another belonged to Flávio’s friend, lawyer Willer Tomaz. Tomaz said he had invited the senator, arranged the flight and covered its entire cost.

Following the report, Flávio said he had not known about Vorcaro's connection to the aircraft and that he had been invited by his friend Willer Tomaz.

Another investigation before the STF, overseen by Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes, is examining whether the senator engaged in money laundering through an online betting company.

Flávio was registered as a "master user" of a bank account belonging to a company owned by lawyer Willer Tomaz, who is under investigation on suspicion of money laundering.

According to the Federal Police, this registration gave Flávio "significant operational access" to the bank account and "supports the hypothesis of his possible financial involvement or de facto ownership stake in the company."

Flávio and Willer Tomaz are friends, but both deny having business interests together.

The Federal Police found evidence suggesting that they shared a bank account belonging to Alcazar Holdings, a company owned by Tomaz, after discovering emails exchanged between the lawyer's secretary and a Santander bank employee.

Willer Tomaz. — Foto: Jornal Nacional/ Reprodução

The investigation began in the southern Brazilian state of Rio Grande do Sul, where the Federal Police were investigating suspected illegal transfers of money abroad and money laundering. One of the targets was the online betting platform Blaze. With court authorization, investigators obtained access to Willer Tomaz's private electronic communications.

The investigation was then transferred to the Supreme Federal Court after Flávio Bolsonaro's name appeared in emails obtained during the inquiry. Under Brazilian law, certain high-ranking officials, including sitting senators, are investigated and tried directly by the Supreme Court in specific criminal cases.

Alcazar Holdings owns one of three shares in the private jet used by Flávio Bolsonaro and Willer Tomaz on a flight from Fort Lauderdale, Florida, to Brazil in January 2025.

Willer is also under investigation for his involvement in a multi-billion-reais scheme to defraud benefits from the National Social Security Institute (INSS, in portuguese).

Flávio is also the subject of a Supreme Court investigation into whether he committed criminal defamation against President Lula. In a post published on X, formerly Twitter, on January 3, 2026, Flávio accused the president, who has since been reelected, of crimes including drug trafficking and money laundering. In July, the Federal Police canceled Flávio's scheduled questioning after his lawyers submitted written explanations.

The first round of Brazil's presidential election, held on Sunday, October 4, ended with Senator Flávio Bolsonaro ahead of President Lula. Flávio received 56,104,503 votes (47.03% of valid votes), while Lula, the candidate of the Workers' Party (PT), received 53,879,538 votes (45.16%).

In the runoff election on October 25, following intense campaigning and mobilization by both sides, Lula won with 64,256,232 votes (51.79% of valid votes), while Flávio received 59,826,041 votes (48.21%).

On election day, a court ordered voting hours to be extended by two hours following requests from both campaigns. Lula's party reported public transportation problems in parts of Bahia and other nine states, while Flávio Bolsonaro's campaign cited heavy rain, flooding, landslides and power outages affecting voters in parts of Minas Gerais, Rio Grande do Sul, Paraná, São Paulo and Santa Catarina.

The decision, however, was announced shortly after 5 p.m., when some polling stations had already closed. The ballot boxes that had already been closed could not be reopened.

As a result, fewer than 35,000 thousand votes had been recorded at the polls by 7 p.m. Lula's lead over Flávio Bolsonaro nationwide in Brazil stood at 4.4 million votes.

How does Brazil's two-round presidential election system work? In Brazil, a presidential candidate must receive more than 50% of valid votes to win in the first round. Blank and invalid ballots are excluded from this calculation. If no candidate reaches that threshold, the two candidates with the most votes face each other in a runoff election.

In the runoff, voters choose between those two candidates. Votes from the first round are not carried over, and the candidate who receives the majority of valid votes wins.

After the results were announced, Kassio Nunes Marques, president of the Superior Electoral Court (TSE), the institution responsible for overseeing Brazil's elections, said he had "full confidence in the electoral process" and confirmed the presidential election results.

What does Flávio claim about the election?

In a letter released on Wednesday (October 28), after fleeing Brazil, the senator again declared that he would not recognize the results of the presidential runoff, alleged electoral fraud and claimed to be the "true president of Brazil."

He contradicted the position taken by his own party, the PL, and the official confirmation of the results by electoral authorities.

After publishing the original letter as images on social media, Flávio released a revised version, replacing the phrases "true president of Brazil" and "president-elect" with "leader of Brazil" and "leader," respectively.

On Sunday (October 25), after the results were announced, Flávio criticized the extension of voting hours, even though his own campaign had also requested it. He said that, because of this, it was "impossible to recognize this result."

"What happened is inexplicable. Even according to the words of one of the justices, as reported by the press, the election should have been annulled under the circumstances in which everything happened. And what I have to say now is that it is impossible, impossible to recognize the election results given everything that happened. We will take legal action and seek to have these election annulled," the defeated candidate said.

articles.title: IFRR Campus Novo Paraíso abre 138 vagas para cursos técnicos | G1
articles.standfirst: Unidade oferta três cursos técnicos integrados ao ensino médio: Alimentos, Agropecuária e Aquicultura. Inscrições são gratuitas.
articles.summary: Com inscrições gratuitas até novembro, o IFRR Campus Novo Paraíso oferece 138 vagas em cursos técnicos integrados para estudantes que concluíram o ensino fundamental.
articles.body:
Entrada do Campus Novo Paraíso do Instituto Federal de Roraima (CNP/IFRR) — Foto: IFRR/Divulgação

O campus Novo Paraíso do Instituto Federal de Roraima (CNP/IFRR) abriu 138 vagas, distribuídas entre os cursos técnicos Agropecuária , Alimentos e Aquicultura . As oportunidades são para cursos técnicos integrados ao ensino médio. As aulas começam em janeiro de 2027.

As inscrições são gratuitas e podem ser feitas no período de 26 de outubro a 26 de novembro de 2026, exclusivamente pela internet.

O processo seletivo contempla candidatos das regiões de Rorainópolis (sede e Vila Nova Colina), Rota 10 (São Luiz do Anauá, São João da Baliza e Caroebe), Caracaraí e Vila Novo Paraíso. Veja distribuição das vagas por região:

Rota 210 — São Luiz, São João da Baliza e Caroebe

Para participar do processo seletivo, o candidato deverá ter no máximo 17 anos completos até à data da matrícula e ter concluído o ensino fundamental até esse mesmo período.

No ato da inscrição, o candidato deverá selecionar o curso pretendido e a modalidade de vaga para a qual deseja concorrer.

As vagas estão distribuídas entre ampla concorrência e ações afirmativas, que incluem critérios relacionados à renda familiar, à etnia e às pessoas com deficiência (PcDs).

Durante a inscrição, o candidato deverá indicar um curso técnico integrado ao ensino médio como primeira opção, podendo escolher um segundo e um terceiro como opções adicionais.

A seleção será realizada por meio de análise curricular quantitativa, considerando o desempenho escolar dos candidatos no 6.º, 7.º, 8.º e 9.º anos do ensino fundamental. O resultado final do processo seletivo 2027 será divulgado no dia 7 de janeiro de 2027.

Para auxiliar os candidatos durante o período de inscrição, serão realizados plantões de atendimento em municípios e localidades da região. Confira o cronograma:

10 de novembro — Caracaraí e Vila Novo Paraíso. Em Caracaraí, das 9h às 11h, na Escola Estadual Presidente Castelo Branco. Na Vila Novo Paraíso, das 14h às 16h, na Escola Estadual Padre Calleri;

11 de novembro — Rorainópolis e Vila Nova Colina. Em Rorainópolis, das 9h às 12h, na Escola Municipal Estadual Pe. Eugênio Possamai. Na Vila Nova Colina, das 14h às 16h, na Escola Militarizada Tenente João de Azevedo Cruz;

12 de novembro — São Luiz do Anauá e São João da Baliza. Em São Luiz do Anauá, das 9h às 11h, na Escola Estadual Alan Kardec. Em São João da Baliza, das 14h às 16h, na Escola Estadual Henrique Dias.

Os candidatos também devem acompanhar as principais datas previstas no edital:

26 de outubro a 26 de novembro de 2026: período de inscrições pela internet.

9 de dezembro de 2026: divulgação do resultado preliminar.

15 de dezembro de 2026: convocação dos candidatos autodeclarados pretos, pardos ou indígenas para a banca de verificação da autodeclaração.

1.º de fevereiro de 2027: previsão de início das aulas do ano letivo de 2027.

Leia outras notícias do estado no g1 Roraima .

articles.title: New polls have more good news for Democrats’ Senate hopes
articles.summary: New surveys confirm just how much Democrats have expanded the Senate map in the 2026 midterm elections.
articles.body:
New surveys confirm just how much Democrats have expanded the Senate map in the 2026 midterm elections.

The New York Times/Siena polls — the first high-quality surveys in some states — show Democrats with a bona fide pickup opportunity in South Carolina and possibly another one in Florida. The Minnesota survey, meanwhile, suggests that GOP hopes of an unlikely pickup there might have been dashed.

One poll in a given state should not be oversold. (And despite Democratic momentum, many races this year are within the margin of error .) But given the dearth of polling in these three particular states — and the stakes of each race this year — the new surveys are worth delving into.

The big news is that appointed GOP Sen. Darline Graham and Democrat Annie Andrews are tied at 48% among likely voters in South Carolina.

It's the first high-quality public poll of the state, and it suggests the race is not just potentially winnable for Democrats, but something of a toss-up, which is astounding in a state President Donald Trump won by 18 points in 2024.

It comes after another Times/Siena poll showed a dead heat in Kansas — a state Trump won by 16 points.

And it's clear why the South Carolina race is close: Republicans nominated a Trump-picked candidate with major qualification questions looming over her.

While likely voters said by 13 points that Andrews (who is a physician) has the "right experience to be an effective senator," they say by 7 points that Graham (the previously largely unknown sister of the late GOP Sen. Lindsey Graham) does not .

Among independents, 59% say Andrews has the right experience, while just 31% say Graham does.

While 62% of Democrats strongly agree that Andrews has the right experience, only 35% of Republicans strongly agree that Graham does.

That's a brutal assessment from Graham's own party.

All of which helps explain why Andrews leads 57%-37% among independents and even pulls 7% of Republican likely voters.

The data also suggests that GOP attempts to paint Andrews as an extremist — largely by invoking her past comments on transgender rights and using an anti-transgender slur against her — have so far fallen flat. Just 39% of likely voters in this conservative state say she's too far to the left.

There's not yet high-quality polling in some other red states where the GOP could be feeling nervous — like Nebraska and even Mississippi, where Trump appeared on Monday. But the Times/Siena polls in Kansas and South Carolina show that Democrats have lots of opportunities.

Another big finding was a poll suggesting Democrats don't have too much to worry about in Minnesota. Up until now, the limited evidence had suggested the state, which backed Kamala Harris by 4 points, was something of a Democratic headache .

The New York Times/Siena survey shows Democratic Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan leading Republican former TV sportscaster Michele Tafoya 54%-40% .

The poll does suggest voters have real concerns about Flanagan being too far to the left, with even 17% of her own supporters saying that about her. She's barely winning any GOP votes — unlike many other Democratic Senate candidates . And she's not especially popular.

But the poll suggests the electorate could just be too friendly to Democrats for any of that to matter.

Democrats lead by 18 points on the generic ballot in the state, and 57% of likely voters have a strongly unfavorable view of Trump.

Even if the Minnesota electorate doesn't wind up being quite as blue as that, Tafoya would seem to face an uphill battle in what looks like a good Democratic year. Flanagan even leads by double digits — 54%-39% — among independents.

A third survey seems to confirm that Florida — which has trended quite Republican in the Trump era — is a second-tier target for Democrats.

The poll shows GOP Sen. Ashley Moody leading Democratic state Rep. Angie Nixon by 6 points, 50-44% . It follows a University of North Florida poll last week that put Moody up by a similar 4-point margin, 49%-45% .

Republicans will be happy their lead remains outside the margin of error.

But that's still competitive. Despite this state being widely written off when Democrats nominated Nixon, a member of the Democratic Socialists of America, just 37% of likely voters say she's too far to the left. And Nixon leads 52%-38% among independents.

It would seem difficult for Nixon to get over the hump in a state that has trended so Republican. But at the very least, the New York Times/Siena poll suggests the governor's race is in play.

It shows GOP Rep. Byron Donalds at 48% and Democratic former Rep. David Jolly at 44% — a 4-point margin that is very close to the poll's 3.9-point margin of error.

Even losing the governor's race in Florida would be a major GOP setback.

For more CNN news and newsletters create an account at CNN.com

articles.title: 'Radical Left Lunatic' judge Trump wanted impeached takes up Ilhan Omar warrant fight
articles.summary: Judge James Boasberg, a frequent Trump legal foe, now oversees the fight to unseal the FBI search warrant used in the raid on Rep. Ilhan Omar's home.
articles.body:
A federal judge who has become a frequent legal thorn in the side of President Donald Trump and his allies is now presiding over a fight to unseal the warrant used to search the home of Rep. Ilhan Omar , D-Minn.

The battle over whether to unseal the search warrant comes amid two separate federal investigations into the Democratic congresswoman stemming from concerns about discrepancies between financial disclosures filed a year apart and allegations that her father committed fraud when completing immigration paperwork. Omar immigrated to the United States from Somalia in 1995, when she was 12 years old. Investigators are examining whether her father misstated her age on his citizenship paperwork in 2000, potentially allowing her to obtain citizenship through him as a minor.

Trump, a longtime foe of the progressive congresswoman, has been vocal in his attacks against Omar, having also accused her of committing immigration fraud by allegedly marrying her brother — referring to her first husband, Ahmed Nur Said Elmi. In the weeks following the Oct. 12 raid on Omar's Washington, D.C., home, Trump called for Omar to be "put in jail."

But the fight over whether to unseal the records is being overseen by Chief Judge James Boasberg of the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, an Obama appointee and longtime target of Trump. In March 2025, after Boasberg temporarily blocked deportation flights carrying alleged Venezuelan gang members, Trump called him a "Radical Left Lunatic of a Judge, a troublemaker and agitator" and called for his impeachment. Trump also accused Boasberg of bias, saying it was "virtually impossible for me to get an Honest Ruling in D.C."

The raid on Omar's home came just weeks before the midterm elections, as alleged fraud in Minnesota's social services programs had become a major political issue in the state.

Days after Department of Homeland Security Investigations and the FBI conducted a raid on Omar's home under a search warrant issued by U.S. Magistrate Judge Matthew Sharbaugh, three separate requests were made to unseal the warrant — by the New York Times; Judicial Watch, a conservative watchdog group; and 14 press organizations.

Boasberg ordered the Justice Department to defend its position on keeping the warrant sealed in response to a consolidated request from the Times and 14 press organizations by Oct. 22, but he extended the deadline following a Justice Department request to wait until the search warrant was "fully executed."

The Justice Department argued that releasing the information could compromise the integrity of the investigation.

"This request sounds rash because it is rash," Pirro wrote. "The Court should reject it without prejudice for renewal after the search warrant has been fully executed and a charging decision is made public."

The filing indicated that the Justice Department was still in the process of executing the search warrant, while other details about the investigation and warrant records remained redacted from the public record.

But the Times and other media groups argue that the physical search occurred weeks ago and that any sensitive information in the warrant should be redacted rather than the entire warrant being withheld.

Meanwhile, Omar is engaged in a separate dispute with the Justice Department. Her attorneys have demanded the return of property seized from her home, arguing that agents violated protections for her congressional work. They have also alleged that agents failed to provide her with a copy of the warrant and prevented her from contacting her attorneys during the search.

Boasberg's oversight of efforts to unseal the records follows a series of decisions that have drawn criticism from Trump and his allies. In June 2025, he ordered federal agencies to preserve Signal messages exchanged by senior officials while discussing U.S. military strikes in Yemen, saying the communications could constitute federal records. During the Biden administration's Arctic Frost investigation, he signed nondisclosure orders barring phone carriers from notifying Republican lawmakers that prosecutors had subpoenaed their records.

Boasberg also drew criticism over his sentencing of former FBI attorney Kevin Clinesmith. Clinesmith pleaded guilty to altering an email used in an application to the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court to renew surveillance of Carter Page, a former Trump campaign adviser suspected of acting as a Russian agent.

Boasberg, who previously served a seven-year term on the FISA Court, said Clinesmith's alteration of the email undermined the court's integrity but was a misguided mistake that provided Clinesmith no personal benefit. He sentenced Clinesmith to 12 months of probation and 400 hours of community service.

Boasberg said in his sentencing decision that he believed Clinesmith's role at the center of a years-long media "hurricane" had provided sufficient punishment.

U.S. District Judge James Boasberg is seen in an official portrait in Washington, D.C., on March 16, 2023.

articles.title: Carta golpista isola Flávio, que perde apoio até entre líderes da direita e enfraquece oposição bolsonarista a Lula | G1
articles.body:
De possível vítima, como pretendia se vender, Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) virou um golpista ao divulgar uma carta se proclamando o verdadeiro presidente eleito do Brasil.

Aliados do candidato derrotado não apoiaram sua decisão publicamente. Reservadamente, se mostraram decepcionados com a atitude do senador do PL e disseram que ele perde todas as condições de se transformar no líder da oposição , o que ele acabou colocando na versão final do documento que repercutiu muito mal no Brasil.

De Tarcísio Gomes de Freitas (Republicanos), passando por Rogério Marinho (PL) e chegando a partidos como União Brasil, PSD, PSDB e MDB, todos repudiaram a carta golpista.

Flávio Bolsonaro desembarca nos EUA — Foto: Eva Marie Uzcategui/Reuters

O presidente do PL, Valdemar Costa Neto, vai conversar nesta quinta-feira (29) com o ex-presidente Jair Bolsonaro (PL) e analisar, com ele, a péssima repercussão da fuga e da divulgação da carta de Flávio Bolsonaro.

Valdemar teme um enfraquecimento do PL exatamente no momento em que seu partido ganhou força depois das eleições. A senadora eleita Michelle Bolsonaro pode ocupar esse espaço de líder do bolsonarismo, mas os enteados não querem que isso aconteça.

Enquanto isso, o governador de São Paulo, Tarcísio Gomes de Freitas, foi claro, é preciso respeitar o resultado das eleições e seguir em frente.

Rogério Marinho (PL-RN), Flávio Bolsonaro (PL-RJ) — Foto: Andressa Anholete/Agência Senado

Coordenador da campanha do PL, Rogério Marinho disse não ter provas de fraudes, reconheceu que o candidato derrotado tem motivos para estar indignado, mas que era preciso se preparar para fazer oposição ao quarto mandato de Lula.

Até o União Brasil, que estava no barco de Flávio Bolsonaro, repudiou o ato do senador.

Até entre evangélicos Flávio Bolsonaro não teve apoio. Líderes evangélicos não concordaram com o teor da carta golpista e disseram que o momento é de seguir em frente.

Apoio mesmo, Flávio Bolsonaro só teve da bancada radical do PL na Câmara dos Deputados, que, apesar de numerosa, corre o risco de ficar isolada como o candidato derrotado.

articles.title: Valdemar Costa Neto reprova carta de Flávio Bolsonaro | G1
articles.standfirst: Carta com teor golpista foi publicada pelo senador após desembarcar nos Estados Unidos. Flávio Bolsonaro contrariou proibição do Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF) de deixar o país.
articles.summary: Valdemar Costa Neto criticou a postura de Flávio Bolsonaro, que publicou uma carta com teor golpista após descumprir ordem do STF e viajar para os Estados Unidos.
articles.body:
O presidente do PL, Valdemar Costa Neto, afirmou nesta quinta-feira (29) que não gostou da carta publicada por Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) nesta quarta-feira (28) em que o senador, derrotado pelo presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) nas eleições, não reconhece o resultado e se autointitula "líder do Brasil".

A carta foi publicada nessa quarta (28) nas redes de Flávio após o senador desembarcar nos Estados Unidos com a família, contrariando decisão do Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF) que o proibiu de deixar o país.

Após a primeira versão, o parlamentar apagou a postagem e substituiu por uma nova carta em que troca as expressões "verdadeiro presidente do Brasil" e "presidente eleito" por "líder do Brasil" e "líder" .

Flávio, no entanto, manteve os trechos em que não reconhece o resultado do pleito e afirma que as eleições foram roubadas.

“Não gostei. Não gostei”, afirmou Valdemar ao chegar ao condomínio do ex-presidente Jair Bolsonaro para uma visita autorizada pelo ministro do Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF), Alexandre de Moraes.

Presidente nacional do PL, Valdemar Costa Neto — Foto: Beto Barata/PL/Divulgação

As alegações, divulgadas sem apresentação de provas, contrariam a postura do PL, partido de Flávio Bolsonaro e presidido por Valdemar, que reconheceu o resultado nas urnas.

Além disso, contrastam com a confirmação da vitória de Lula pelo Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE). O PL reconheceu o resultado eleitoral e pediu esclarecimentos à Justiça.

Lideranças da direita e partidos se manifestaram contra a carta com teor golpista. O governador de São Paulo, Tarcísio de Freitas (Republicanos), afirmou que o senador deve respeitar o resultado das urnas e seguir em frente.

Partidos como União Brasil, PSD, PSDB e MDB também repudiaram o conteúdo da carta e defenderam o resultado das urnas.

Valdemar deu a declaração à imprensa antes de visita ao ex-presidente Jair Bolsonaro (PL), detido em prisão domiciliar após ser condenado pelo Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF) por tramar um golpe de Estado no país.

Segundo o blog do Valdo Cruz, no g1 , o presidente do partido irá analisar, ao lado do ex-presidente, a péssima repercussão da fuga e da divulgação da carta de Flávio Bolsonaro.

Valdemar teme um enfraquecimento do PL exatamente no momento em que seu partido ganhou força depois das eleições . A senadora eleita Michelle Bolsonaro (PL) pode ocupar esse espaço de líder do bolsonarismo, mas os enteados não querem que isso aconteça.

articles.title: Davi Alcolumbre negocia indulto a Bolsonaro por reeleição no Senado | G1
articles.standfirst: Nos bastidores, presidente do Senado defende pacificação do país, mas integrantes do PL veem na negociação uma estratégia para fortalecer sua candidatura e acenar a bolsonaristas .
articles.summary: Davi Alcolumbre negocia o fim da pressão contra o STF e um possível indulto a Bolsonaro para neutralizar a oposição e garantir sua reeleição no Senado Federal.
articles.body:
Jair Bolsonaro (PL) e Davi Alcolumbre (União-AP) — Foto: Jornal Nacional/ Reprodução e Ton Molina/Agência Senado

O presidente do Senado, Davi Alcolumbre (União-AP), avalia a possibilidade de negociar um acordo político que envolva conter a pressão por impeachment de ministros do Supremo Tribunal Federal ( STF ) e discutir um eventual indulto ao ex-presidente Jair Bolsonaro (PL).

O foco é o componente de sobrevivência política nessa movimentação: a tentativa de construir um acordo que viabilize sua reeleição à presidência do Senado.

A avaliação feita por esses interlocutores é que, caso Alcolumbre consiga uma aproximação com o grupo de Bolsonaro, sua situação na disputa pelo comando da Casa muda significativamente.

Isso porque um entendimento com o bolsonarismo poderia dificultar a construção de uma candidatura alternativa, especialmente Rogerio Marinho (PL-RN) ou a da senadora Tereza Cristina (PP-MS), nomes considerados por uma ala da direita para a presidência do Senado.

Na prática, Alcolumbre tentaria neutralizar a resistência do PL à sua permanência no cargo, oferecendo como contrapartida uma negociação em torno de duas pautas sensíveis para o bolsonarismo: a situação judicial de Jair Bolsonaro e a pressão contra ministros do Supremo.

O discurso público seria o da pacificação institucional.

Nos bastidores, Alcolumbre tem argumentado que o país precisa de pacificação e que é necessário construir um novo ambiente de diálogo entre os Poderes depois das eleições.

Nos bastidores, porém, integrantes do próprio PL reconhecem que a negociação também atenderia aos interesses eleitorais de Alcolumbre dentro do Senado.

O que está na mesa, portanto, é a possibilidade de um acordo político que combine a redução das tensões entre o Congresso e o Supremo com a construção de uma maioria capaz de garantir a reeleição de Alcolumbre.

Ainda não há acordo fechado. Mas a hipótese já é discutida nos bastidores e expõe como a disputa pelo comando do Senado se mistura às negociações sobre o futuro político e judicial de Bolsonaro.

articles.title: US midterms: Five days to go – What the polls say as Trump, Harris campaign
articles.summary: With five days until the US midterms, here’s what polls show, the latest campaign news and what’s next.
articles.body:
With five days to go before the United States midterms , Democrats are ahead in national polls, but several Senate races remain close.

President Donald Trump, former President Barack Obama and Vice President JD Vance were out campaigning on Wednesday in Ohio, Georgia and North Carolina, as both parties fight for control of Congress.

What do the latest polls say about the US midterms?

Democrats lead Republicans by 51.4 percent to 43.2 percent, a gap of 8.2 percentage points, according to RealClearPolling’s national polling average.

But the national lead is not reflected in every Senate race.

In Texas, where Democrats haven’t won a Senate election since 1988, Democrat James Talarico leads Republican Ken Paxton with 48.5 percent to 46.7 percent, according to the poll aggregator.

In Michigan , Democrat Abdul El-Sayed has widened his lead over Republican Mike Rogers to seven percentage points, according to a Mitchell Research poll conducted for CBS Detroit.

The October 26-27 survey found El-Sayed leading Rogers 51 percent to 44 percent, up from a 4.2-point advantage earlier this month.

RealClearPolling showed a narrower race, with El-Sayed at 48 percent and Rogers at 46 percent.

Despite that lead, Democrats are continuing to campaign for support among young voters in Michigan.

“We need everybody and young people are a huge part of the coalition and could really be the difference-maker on November 3rd,” Will Lawrence, a Democratic candidate hoping to win Michigan’s 7th Congressional District from the Republicans, told Al Jazeera.

Democratic Congressman Maxwell Frost, who travelled from Florida to campaign for El-Sayed, said face-to-face conversations with voters were particularly important.

“Everyone’s seen the negative bigoted ads and Islamophobic ads, but what hasn’t happened is everyone hasn’t had person-to-person conversation about why Abdul is the right senator for Michigan,” he said.

Republicans are also trying to reach young voters, with one supporter telling Al Jazeera: “I think there’s definitely a movement that people don’t realise in Gen Z that is turning more conservative.”

Beyond Michigan, some voters told Al Jazeera they were frustrated with both parties.

“Each party wants to be in power and I think they’ll say what they think they want their voters to hear,” one voter said in Lexington, Kentucky.

Democratic strategist Joel Rubin described the midterms as a potential “protest election”, with many Democratic voters looking to limit Trump’s power.

“I think that overwhelmingly American voters who will vote Democratic are voting because they want to put a check on President Trump’s power,” he said.

Republican strategist Suhail Khan said Trump was losing support among a number of his own voters, who were frustrated by rising fuel prices, rents and mortgage costs.

“I keep voting and I’m independent, I vote both sides … I’m so frustrated and out of hope,” another voter said in Gettysburg, Pennsylvania.

Democrats are hoping to overturn Republican majorities in both chambers of Congress, but the Senate presents a bigger challenge.

They need a net gain of three seats in the House of Representatives and four in the Senate, where Republicans currently hold 53 of the 100 seats. Democrats hold 47, including two independents who caucus with them.

Democrats need to reach 51 seats to take control, but the path to a Senate majority is not simple.

“Even the most optimistic of Republicans will tell you that it’s going to be pretty tough for the GOP to hold on to the House of Representatives,” Al Jazeera’s Scott McLean said. “Different story when it comes to the US Senate, though.”

McLean said that even if Democrats win North Carolina and Ohio and hold on to their current seats, they would still be two seats short of the 51 needed for a majority.

Alaska and Texas could help close that gap. But Republicans are also hoping to win Michigan, where the race remains tight.

Taking control of the House of Representatives alone would still have significant consequences for Trump. If the Democrats flip the House, they can block parts of his legislative agenda and launch investigations into his administration.

They would also be able to call administration officials to testify before congressional committees, although the White House could challenge those demands.

What’s happened on the US midterm campaign trail in the past 24 hours?

Trump was in Ohio campaigning for Republican Senator Jon Husted, who is facing former Democratic Senator Sherrod Brown.

During the rally, Trump defended Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy following backlash over an advertisement featuring the estranged mother of his Democratic rival, Amy Acton.

Ramaswamy was being treated “very unfairly”, Trump said. “How the hell is that his problem?”

Trump also spoke about Jeffrey Epstein after protesters interrupted his speech, saying he had expelled the late sex offender from his Mar-a-Lago club two decades ago.

Meanwhile, in Georgia, former President Obama joined Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff and gubernatorial candidate Keisha Lance Bottoms.

Obama criticised Republicans for their reaction to his recent Cheesecake Factory joke about White House renovations, saying they were more concerned about that than the rising cost of living.

“These are not serious people. They don’t have solutions to actual problems,” he said.

Vance also rallied in North Carolina, where former Governor Roy Cooper is facing Republican Michael Whatley in the Senate race.

What’s next for Trump, Democrats and Republicans?

Trump is scheduled to campaign in South Carolina on Thursday at 16:30 GMT, before heading to Florida on Friday and Kansas on Saturday.

South Carolina is among the Republican-held Senate seats Democrats are targeting, although the party faces a difficult contest in a traditionally conservative state.

In Texas, Vice President JD Vance will hold a rally in Weatherford at 17:15 GMT, with Republican candidate Ken Paxton facing a close Senate race against Democrat James Talarico.

Talarico will also be campaigning on Thursday in Dallas, at 00:00 GMT on Friday (7pm Thursday local time).

Al Jazeera’s Phil Lavelle reported from Texas that Republicans are particularly concerned about turnout in rural areas, where 21 percent of registered voters had cast their ballots, compared with 24 percent in the more heavily populated metropolitan areas.

Meanwhile, former Vice President Kamala Harris is expected to campaign in Georgia, where Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff is defending his seat against Republican Mike Collins.

Georgia’s early in-person voting ends on Friday as both parties make their final push before Election Day.

articles.title: HUGH HEWITT: The hidden advantage that could turn Senate toss-ups into GOP wins
articles.summary: Susan Collins' seniority advantage and key Senate races from Ohio to Minnesota could determine GOP control as Trump campaigns across the country.
articles.body: Which candidates for Senate are in a better position to help their state and, by extension, their citizens in the six years ahead? This is the question voters in every state with a contested Senate seat should ask themselves before they vote between now and the close of voting Tuesday. Example number one is Maine, where Senator Susan Collins is matched against Troy Jackson. Jackson is the man picked by Maine’s Democratic Party — not the voters — after Graham Platner crashed, burned and withdrew from the race on July 10. The party’s state committee picked Jackson even though he had finished third in the Democratic governor’s primary the same day Platner won his primary. Polls rate the Maine race as a toss-up, but polls at the close in 2020 had Collins behind by at least four percentage points, and she in fact won by more than 8%. MORNING GLORY: THE DEMOCRATS HAVE A 'FANATIC FOUR' OF EXTREMIST SENATE CANDIDATES Maine voters are unlikely to surrender the seniority Collins holds — she is chair of the powerful Senate Appropriations Committee — for a rookie who would rank tied for last in the currency that matters the most in the Senate: the incumbent’s years served in the body. Add to that reality the fact that every Mainer seems to know the senator at least in passing and that communities across the state have benefited from the influence she has accumulated over more than 10,000 consecutive roll call votes, and Collins is poised to win. Again. In South Carolina, Sen. Darline Graham has been serving since her brother Lindsey died. That gives her a leg up on new senators elected this year, and in a state that went for Donald Trump by 18% in 2024, it’s very likely Graham will return for a full six-year term. Ohio’s incumbent Sen. Jon Husted has been in the Senate since January 2025. As a member of the majority, he’s in a position to deliver more for the Buckeye State than the recycled Democrat Sherrod Brown, who was ousted by Ohio voters two years ago after collecting government paychecks for almost 50 years. Brown’s very liberal career lost touch with an Ohio electorate that went for Trump in 2024 by more than 11 points. Husted is the best candidate to deliver for Ohio. In Michigan, either Republican Mike Rogers or Democrat Abdul El-Sayed would be a freshman senator, but El-Sayed’s white-hot radicalism will put him in a corner of the Senate that is empty except for Bernie Sanders. Rogers, by contrast, is a mainstream, moderate Republican with 14 years of experience in the House. Expect Rogers to receive a warm welcome from the Senate GOP, which is eyeing Michigan as a battleground state in the 2028 presidential election. FOX NEWS POLL: MICHIGAN VOTERS SPLIT BETWEEN EL-SAYED AND ROGERS There’s a reason why most contenders for the GOP nomination have been to Michigan to lend Rogers a hand. Pennsylvania’s Senator Dave McCormick was in the Wolverine State this week, and not surprisingly, McCormick’s name is in the mix for 2028. That's also true for Texas Republican Sen. Ted Cruz, who seems to have been everywhere this election cycle helping everyone (as a prospective candidate for the presidency does). Cruz was in Alaska on October 17 to give an assist to Sen. Dan Sullivan, who is a two-term incumbent with enormous ability to deliver for Alaskans. Democratic nominee Mary Peltola, by contrast, would be a freshman in the minority party if, as I expect, the GOP retains the majority. That’s a terrible trade and one that it is doubtful most Alaskans want to make. President Trump’s campaign trip to Alaska — rare for a sitting president — was intended to juice turnout there and to focus attention on the dirty tricks at work up north. A second "decoy" Dan Sullivan was planted on the four-choice ballot in the hopes of draining even a few votes from the real Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska’s weird ranked-choice voting scheme. PELTOLA ALLIES WORKED TO RECRUIT SPOILER CANDIDATES IN ALASKA SENATE RACE, REPORT SAYS The real Dan Sullivan, the retired Marine Corps colonel on the Armed Services Committee with great seniority, is asking all voters, "Don’t rank Mary," to counteract the trickery. The electorate’s about a quarter of a million people. It’s a savvy bunch because the federal government matters so much in our 49th state. Expect the real Sen. Dan Sullivan to pull through. President Trump won Alaska by more than 13% in 2024. He also won Texas and Iowa by more than 13%, which tells us that while Sen. Sullivan’s seniority will help him, even first-time candidates Ken Paxton in Texas and Ashley Hinson in Iowa should prevail against Democratic first-time nominees in both states, even in the "tough environment" of a president’s sixth year in office. President Trump has been to both states this week to energize the base. Whatever the polls say — and polls say both races are toss-ups — Paxton and Hinson appear to be in good shape and rising in the polls, and both would be joining a majority in the Senate, not the minority with vastly diminished powers. Kansas went for Donald Trump by more than 16% two years ago. Its farmers have been hit hard by the high cost of diesel, but they know Sen. Roger Marshall has the seniority to help on the "Ag Bill" and deliver relief for the state. The nice pastor running against the nice Dr. Marshall doesn’t. The same is true for Sen. Pete Ricketts in Nebraska. GOP SENATE MAJORITY FACES FRESH UNCERTAINTY AS 2 KEY RACES TIGHTEN DAYS BEFORE MIDTERMS Which brings us finally to Minnesota, which is a deep blue state but one that nominated a far-far-to-the-left Democratic candidate in Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan, whose eight years in that state job coincided with the massive fraud scandals in Minnesota and soaring violence among gangs of Somali-American youths. The Democratic Farmer-Labor Party decided to go way left even as the GOP nominated the sparkling political "Rookie of the Year" in Michele Tafoya. Michigan might have the most-watched race because there’s never been an extremist like El-Sayed so close to winning a Senate race before, but the biggest upset could come in Minnesota, with Gopher State voters returning to the tradition of sending their occasional Republican to the Senate. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION American polling is as broken as Israeli polling, which just face-planted in Israel’s elections Tuesday. (Prime Minister Netanyahu emerged with the largest party and the largest coalition, which very few, if any, major polls saw coming.) Trusting polls to place bets on the prediction markets for American Senate races is as foolish as using the Farmers’ Almanac to plan your vacation in an El Niño year. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The enormous advantage of seniority plus the record amount and pace of campaigning by President Trump don’t combine to leave the GOP anxiety-free. But Republicans surely don’t take their cues from legacy media and pollsters, which are, again, almost all openly tilted toward Democrats. The vote will be intensely interesting, but if "toss-ups" turn out to be blowouts in red states, don’t be surprised. CLICK HERE TO READ MORE FROM HUGH HEWITT

articles.title: Obama and Trump spar at rallies in Georgia and Ohio: Key takeaways
articles.summary: Obama and Trump traded barbs over the Iran war, tariffs and the White House ballroom ahead of the US midterm elections.
articles.body:
Former US President Barack Obama and President Donald Trump held rival campaign rallies in Georgia and Ohio on Wednesday, trading criticism over the war in Iran, tariffs and the economy just five days before midterm elections.

Here are some of the key takeaways from their rallies:

Obama said the Iran war has made Americans less safe

“The current president chose to make a series of bad decisions, the most important of which was to start an unnecessary war that nobody asked for and nobody voted for,” Obama said during a campaign rally in Atlanta, Georgia.

The United States and Israel launched strikes on Iran on February 28, targeting Tehran as well as the country’s nuclear and military facilities, and killing Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei and several high-ranking officials. Tehran responded with attacks on US military assets across the region and closed the Strait of Hormuz, a vital route for about one-fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas supplies.

Although a ceasefire was reached in April – and a memorandum of understanding was signed in June – both fell apart, while efforts to secure lasting peace have stalled over Iran’s nuclear programme, US sanctions and the reopening of the strait.

The US media has also reported that the US is low on weapons – particularly its Patriot missile interceptors.

“We have run down our stock of missiles, making us more vulnerable. And Iran now has veto power over the Strait of Hormuz where much of the world’s oil goes through to get to consumers,” Obama told supporters.

“This is the reason why the price of oil is up. This is the reason why the price of diesel is up. The price of just about everything is up,” he added.

“Contrary to the promises and statements and declarations that were made seven months ago, this war is not over.”

Obama again criticised Trump’s trade tariffs, which he launched against global trading partners shortly after taking office in early 2025. Obama argued these have increased the cost of goods for American consumers rather than delivering the economic benefits promised by the administration.

“Economists said when you impose tariffs, consumers pay the tab,” Obama said. “And that’s exactly what happened.”

“Rather than having the tariffs bring down deficits like he said he would, we’re now running a debt to the tune of $40 trillion .”

In particular, he singled out Trump’s ongoing dispute with Canada, one of the US’s largest trading partners.

The two countries have been locked in a trade war, with Trump announcing 50 percent tariffs on Canadian vehicles and auto parts from January 2027. Canada retaliated with its own matching tariffs as talks fell apart in August.

“And the big trade war he’s waging now is that well-known evil empire, that historical adversary of the United States, Canada,” Obama said.

He also criticised Trump’s approach to US allies and Russia.

“While we’re alienating key allies like Canada, the White House is bending the knee to Vladimir Putin of Russia and selling out Ukrainians who are fighting for their freedom and democracy.”

Obama revisited his Cheesecake Factory joke

Obama again made fun of Trump’s White House renovations, saying the president appeared more concerned about a joke he made over the weekend than rising prices.

At an earlier rally , Obama had criticised Trump’s plans for a new ballroom, changes to the Rose Garden and the addition of gold decorations.

“He seems very focused on home renovations. He should be on HGTV,” Obama joked. “He’s got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory, just gold everywhere.”

In Georgia, Obama returned to the joke. “The president wasn’t even mad about the Saddam Hussein comparison. That part didn’t bother him,” Obama said.

“But he was very upset about the Cheesecake Factory comments.”

Obama joked that the White House had gone to great lengths to respond. “They mobilised a whole-of-government response to that joke. Not to inflation, but to that joke.”

He also talked about his own fondness for the restaurant chain.

“I lived at Chuck-E-Cheese and California Pizza Kitchen and the Cheesecake Factory. That was my jam for about a decade.”

Returning to Trump’s renovations, Obama added: “He is literally doing arts and crafts while we are fighting a war and trying to deal with out-of-control prices.”

Obama closed his speech reflecting on American political culture, saying the country’s problems go beyond inflation, economic inequality and government policy.

“It’s not just about economics. It’s not just about prices. It’s about values,” he said. “There is a moral component to the choices we face right now.”

Obama warned that dishonesty and intimidation were undermining public life.

“We are not going to fix the system that’s broken. We’re not going to unrig our economy so long as we’ve got a culture where anything goes, where people in the highest offices of the land think it’s OK to lie and cheat and bully.”

He referenced a 1954 sermon by civil rights leader Martin Luther King Jr, who called on Americans to rediscover values society had abandoned.

“If we are to go forward today, we’ve got to go back and rediscover some mighty precious values that we’ve left behind,” Obama quoted King as saying.

Trump attacked Obama’s Iran nuclear deal

Trump defended his military campaign against Iran and criticised the 2015 nuclear deal with Iran reached under Barack Obama.

The deal limited how much uranium Iran could enrich and stockpile, and allowed international inspectors to monitor its nuclear facilities. Trump pulled the US out in 2018, saying the deal did not go far enough and failed to address Iran’s missile programme and activities in the region.

“I terminated Barack Hussein Obama’s JCPOA or the Iran nuclear deal, which was a road to a nuclear weapon for Iran and one of the dumbest deals I’ve ever seen in my life,” Trump said.

Trump claimed US military operations had since destroyed Iran’s nuclear enrichment capacity and much of its military, including 159 naval vessels.

“We obliterated Iran’s nuclear enrichment capacity with Operation Midnight Hammer and Operation Epic Fury,” he said.

Turning to the Strait of Hormuz, Trump claimed oil shipments had increased and suggested renaming the waterway after himself. “We’re going to call it the Trump Strait,” he said.

The strait, between Iran and Oman, connects the Gulf to the Gulf of Oman and the Arabian Sea. Before the war, about a fifth of the world’s oil consumption passed through it.

Early in his remarks in Chillicothe, Ohio, Trump was interrupted by a protester shouting about Jeffrey Epstein.

Trump rarely brings up Epstein, his former friend, but on Wednesday he repeated claims he made last year that he threw Epstein out of his Florida club about two decades ago.

“That was a great thing I did, I must tell you,” Trump said. He added: “I threw Jeffrey Epstein the hell out of Mar-a-Lago.”

Trump then accused Democrats of having ties to Epstein and using the controversy against him. “He was a Democrat,” Trump said.

Trump also claimed the protesters were being paid to disrupt his rallies, without providing evidence.

“These guys are paid protesters. Think of a guy, that guy’s probably 45, 50 years old. They give him $250.”

After he was interrupted by two more protesters, Trump returned to his remarks.

Trump said Venezuela delivered one million barrels of oil

Trump said Venezuela had delivered one million barrels of oil to the US for free following the US military operation that removed Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro from power.

“Venezuela, they don’t like talking about, we just got a million barrels of oil delivered to us free of charge,” Trump said during his rally in Ohio.

The shipment arrived in Corpus Christi, Texas, on Tuesday, nearly 10 months after US forces abducted Maduro during a military operation on January 3 and transferred him to New York to face drug trafficking charges.

Since Maduro’s removal, Washington has been working with Venezuela’s interim government, led by Delcy Rodriguez, to gain greater access to the country’s oil reserves.

Trump described the military operation as a victory and said Washington was now working with Venezuela to expand oil production. “We had a little war with Venezuela. We finished it in one day,” he said.

“And we’re now working with them to produce millions and millions of barrels of oil a week.”

The president in his speech once again defended Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy for a campaign advertisement featuring the estranged mother of Amy Acton, his Democratic opponent for Ohio governor, which has drawn backlash because of the abuse Acton experienced as a child.

“Vivek was treated very unfairly,” Trump said during his Ohio rally. “He had the mother of his opponent say that her daughter was a liar.”

Trump accused the media of treating Ramaswamy differently because he is a Republican.

“The mother said that Amy Acton, the daughter, is a liar. That she’s no good. That she lied about the opponent. How the hell is that his problem?”

Trump defended his White House renovations

After Obama mocked his plans for the White House, Trump said: “President Obama, who doesn’t understand cleanliness. Who doesn’t understand broken cracked stone and sidewalk?”

He said the White House had been in poor condition and that he had personally paid for repairs. “I fixed it very inexpensively. I paid for it myself. I fixed it.”

Because the White House, I think, is the number one symbol of our country. And we can’t have a White House with broken windows, with broken stone that hasn’t been painted in 30 years.”

“It’s never looked more beautiful,” he said.

He also mocked Obama’s record of campaigning for Democratic presidential candidates.

“He got involved with Hillary Clinton … and he lost. He then got involved with Kamala and he lost.”

“They said Obama’s coming. I said that’s good.”

articles.title: Thune goes all-in on campaign trail as Schumer stays on bench, faces rejection from fellow Dems
articles.summary: John Thune campaigns across key states while Chuck Schumer shifts to virtual events and faces growing resistance from his own party's candidates.
articles.body: FREMONT, Neb. — Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., likes to joke that he’ll be whatever his candidates need him to be in order to win their races. "I tell all of our candidates, I'll come out for you or against you, whichever helps you the most," Thune told Fox News Digital. Thune’s tongue-in-cheek response came just before he attended a roundtable in Nebraska alongside Sen. Pete Ricketts, R-Neb., who is running a tight race against independent Dan Osborn. That stop inside a corrugated metal building nestled among row after row of cornfields was among several visits the top Senate Republican has made across the country this cycle. Since the Senate left Washington, D.C., last month to hit the campaign trail, Thune has been busy, hitting key states like Georgia, South Carolina, Florida, Minnesota, Nebraska, Iowa and Ohio. But as Thune racks up miles on the road, Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., has been largely absent. THUNE MAKES BOLD PREDICTION ABOUT REPUBLICANS' SENATE CHANCES AS GOP PULLS MILLIONS FROM KEY RACES Schumer has shifted to virtual events while high-profile surrogates, like former President Barack Obama, former Vice President Kamala Harris and others have descended upon battleground states that could make or break his ambitions of Democratic control of the Senate. His most recent event came earlier this week: a virtual fundraiser for Florida state Rep. Angie Nixon, the Democratic Socialists of America-affiliated nominee running against Sen. Ashley Moody, R-Fla. Many candidates running in key races across the map from Michigan to Mississippi have tried to distance themselves from Schumer or outright said they wouldn’t support him to lead Senate Democrats. SCHUMER SAYS HE'S NOT GOING ANYWHERE, BUT HIS OWN CANDIDATES AREN'T READY TO BACK HIM One of those candidates includes Scott Colom, a district attorney in Mississippi running against Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, R-Miss. The Senate Majority PAC, a super PAC closely aligned with Schumer, has teed up $1.2 million in advertising in the state, but Colom isn’t welcoming the top Senate Democrat with open arms. When asked by Fox News Digital if he would support Schumer should he win his race, Colom said, "I don't want to get into hypotheticals, because I don't know what the options are, who the options are." "But I'll say this, I don't like that our party is represented by two people that live in the same borough," Colom said, referring to Schumer and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y. "We need to have people that understand rural America. You know, that's part of the problem is we don't have enough rural voices in leadership in the Democratic Party, because we have values and we have a vision that might not be the same as the people in New York," he continued. "And we need to make sure our values and visions are part of the Democratic Party." Others, like Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan or Adam Hamilton in Kansas, have been more explicit in saying they won’t support Schumer if they make it to the Senate. SCHUMER, DEMS ARE QUIETLY BETTING BIG ON ONE SLEEPER RACE IN THE DEEP SOUTH Republicans have leaned into that growing schism between Schumer and the ones who could make his wish of a Democratic-controlled Senate come true. "If you look at Republicans, there's not a single Republican running nationally that's saying, ‘Hey, if you elect me, I'll vote against John Thune as leader,’" Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, said. "On the Democrat side, you have virtually every candidate running saying, ‘If you elect me, I will vote against Chuck Schumer.’" "They're going to have a huge problem, because the Democrats are really, really pissed off about Schumer," he continued. "So he's the problem." Meanwhile, as the outlook for control of the Senate remains in the air, Thune has dedicated his time to showing up wherever his candidates need him. "We're getting out and about — It's whatever we can do to help," he said. On the other side of the political coin, Thune argued that the Democratic Party was struggling to find its identity in an election with high stakes for both parties. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP He contended that socialists were the rising faction within the party, which was "creating problems for their leadership. And I think it's in both the House and the Senate, you're having to decide, is that what we want to be? Does that really represent us?" And that ascendant left flank of Schumer’s could cause problems in a political environment that could be leaning Democrats’ way, Thune said. "They've gotten so far left that they really are out of the mainstream of where the country's at," Thune said. "And I think that's going to hurt them in this election in what otherwise might be arguably a decent political environment for them, but I just — their party has really, really drifted."

articles.title: TAYLOR WEYENETH: Final Republican election strategy has two essential elements
articles.summary: Congressional Democrats face internal battles as Democratic Socialists of America members could dictate key decisions in a razor-thin House majority.
articles.body: Fox News’ recent report on how a Democratic majority could expose the limits of the progressive agenda identifies the tension at the center of the next Congress: Democrats could win the House with a coalition of progressive members and moderates elected in competitive districts, then struggle to agree on what their majority should do. Fox’s House rankings also show how narrow that majority could be, while its Senate analysis describes a chamber where a 50-50 split would leave Republicans with the vice president’s tiebreaking vote. For Republicans, the strategic task is clear: hold the Senate, keep House losses as small as possible and make the case for governing around voters’ priorities. A Democratic House would have the authority to investigate the administration. Oversight is a legitimate responsibility, but if Democratic leaders make investigations the organizing principle of their majority, hearings, subpoenas and document disputes could consume the calendar and political attention that Congress needs to address the cost of living, energy prices, border security and national defense. KATHY HOCHUL 'EXCITED' ABOUT PROSPECT OF DEMOCRATS TYING TRUMP UP IN INVESTIGATIONS That choice could also deepen divisions inside the Democratic caucus. In a House majority measured by only a few seats, a small group of members can gain leverage over leadership votes, procedural decisions and the price of passing legislation. Fox's reporting describes how Democratic leaders are already navigating progressive demands alongside the concerns of members from more competitive districts. That is where members of the Democratic Socialists of America, along with other lawmakers aligned with its priorities, could become the party’s outliers. They would not control the entire caucus, but could have an outsized role in deciding the legislative schedule. When the margin is razor-thin, even a handful of members can press leadership for commitments on policy or use a close vote to extract concessions. If Democrats do not go far enough for them, they could slow or block their own party’s agenda. CARVILLE SAYS HE'D RATHER REPUBLICANS KEEP THE HOUSE THAN DEMOCRATS WIN BY FIVE SEATS, HELD 'HOSTAGE' BY DSA Republicans should understand the opportunity. The DSA could dictate key decisions in a Democratic House. The risk for Democratic leaders is a recurring internal negotiation that makes compromise harder and gives moderates another reason to hesitate. If progressives demand more than swing-district members can defend, Republicans can argue that Democratic leaders are spending their majority on intraparty disputes instead of practical results. How the tables would have turned. Keeping the Senate matters for the same reason. A Republican Senate would preserve a check on the House majority, shape judicial and executive confirmations and give bipartisan proposals a place to move if members in both parties are willing to negotiate. A tie would still leave Republicans with effective control through the vice president’s tie-breaking vote. That would not let Republicans pass major legislation on their own. Most bills would still require cooperation across chambers, and many would need broad support in the Senate. But it would keep the chamber from becoming an extension of the House Democratic agenda. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION In the campaign’s final days, Republicans should make the case that pocketbook issues require a Congress focused on governing, not one consumed by investigations or pulled toward the loudest voices in either party. The objective is to keep the House margin close enough that Democrats must answer to their moderates, while retaining a Republican Senate as a check and a forum for bipartisan dealmaking. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Voters should see the stakes clearly: a narrowly divided House, a Senate no faction can dominate, and a Democratic caucus pulled between progressives and members elected in competitive districts. Republicans can close by promising what voters want from Congress: serious debate and workable solutions. If we hold the Senate and limit our House losses, divided government does not have to mean gridlock.

articles.title: Alaska election officials oppose Trump DOJ’s involvement in Senate race
articles.summary: Alaska officials said new revelations in The New York Times about efforts by Democrats to recruit a Senate candidate with the same name as GOP incumbent Sen....
articles.body:
Alaska officials said new revelations in The New York Times about efforts by Democrats to recruit a Senate candidate with the same name as GOP incumbent Sen. Dan S. Sullivan do not change the state's opposition to a Trump administration lawsuit seeking to potentially delay certification of the election.

The Times story , a spokesperson for the Alaska Department of Law told CNN in an email, confirms the "initial concerns" election officials had about the candidacy of Daniel J. Sullivan, a retired teacher, but it has "no impact on the current litigation."

"Placing candidates on the ballot is a matter of state law, not federal law," said spokesperson Sam Curtis, noting that the Alaska Supreme Court has already decided that Daniel J. Sullivan would be on the ballot. The Justice Department, meanwhile, is citing a federal law in the case that "does not dictate what candidates can run in elections and does not authorize the relief the DOJ seeks," Curtis said.

"The Division is bound by the Alaska Supreme Court's order and is committed to running a fair election and assisting voters as needed," Curtis said.

The story published Wednesday rattled one of the country's most competitive Senate races with less than a week until Election Day.

Mary Peltola, the state's former at-large House member, is considered one of Senate Democrats' top recruits of the midterms and her campaign continues to deny any involvement in Daniel J. Sullivan's campaign. Republicans have been concerned enough about the race that both President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance have made trips to Alaska in recent weeks.

Trump, who has complained about the two Sullivan issue for months and said he directed the Justice Department lawsuit last week, piled on with multiple social media posts slamming Peltola over the story, including one that said she "should be removed from the Ballot and prosecuted."

"So should the FAKE Dan Sullivan," Trump wrote on Truth Social. "Nothing else will do!"

The incumbent's campaign accused Peltola in a statement of spending months "gaslighting Alaskans."

"I am pressing my opponent to come clean," Sullivan said while speaking with Fox News' Sean Hannity Wednesday night. "She's been lying for over a year. She's run a campaign about supposed corruption. She's the corrupt one working with DC insiders to trick Alaskans. So what we're going to do is we're going to make sure every single Alaskan knows about this."

Attorney General Todd Blanche on Fox News touted the Times' story as proof that the Justice Department was right in bringing its unprecedented federal lawsuit. But when pressed over whether anything illegal had occurred that gives the DOJ the ability to intervene in the election, which is run by states, Blanche could not say.

The Justice Department on Wednesday told a federal judge it would like to seek answers and evidence from Peltola's campaign regarding the Times report and Sullivan issue, which it called a "conspiracy."

Late Wednesday, Alaska's Republican Gov. Mike Dunleavy also said he was ordering an investigation into whether criminal charges or civil action should be brought over the alleged Democratic efforts to confuse voters.

"Deliberately tricking voters into casting their ballots for someone else strikes at the integrity of our elections," he said on X . "Anyone or any organization found to have broken the law must be held accountable."

Some Democrats noted that Republicans have also meddled in the race to boost spoiler candidates. An array of GOP groups, for example, contributed to a super PAC that attacked Peltola in the primary and promoted a lesser-known Democratic candidate and a Green Party candidate.

"This is basically a more extreme version of what the parties do all the time, which is try to find a candidate on the other side who can siphon votes away from the major party competitor," election law specialist Rick Hasen told CNN. "And, you know, you can't really hold someone responsible for impure motives."

Dean Franita Tolson of the University of Southern California Gould School of Law said the Times reporting doesn't give the Department of Justice's lawsuit any more credence.

"At the end of the day, the federal government should not try to block certification of a race because they don't like the outcome," she said.

"It, I think, makes the Peltola campaign look bad," Derek Muller, a law professor at the University of Notre Dame Law School, added. "I think it will adversely affect her in the eyes of some voters, but from litigation perspective, I think it really won't affect things at this stage."

This story has been updated with additional information.

For more CNN news and newsletters create an account at CNN.com
authors: Tierney Sneed, Patrick Svitek, Tori B. Powell, CNN
