articles.title: Omar’s midterm rival exposes 'vicious' Somali gangs amid immigration probe into embattled rep
articles.summary: The Republican challenger John Nagel says Somali gangs are running guns in Minneapolis and slams Rep. Ilhan Omar amid a federal immigration probe.
articles.body: MINNEAPOLIS — The Republican running an underdog bid to unseat embattled Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., in Minnesota's 5th Congressional District, tore into his progressive opponent after her Washington, D.C., home was raided a month before the midterm election. John Nagel said it should be easy for the Somali-born congresswoman to clear up any public misunderstandings of her immigration status amid a federal investigation into alleged fraud and said that Omar views herself as Somali first, American second. He also claimed that Minneapolis has a "terrorist problem" and a gun-running operation, and called for a task force to crack down on the Somali gang violence. "We have two problems in Minnesota. We have a terrorist problem, which you saw with the Mall of America — thank God that the FBI actually took care of that before anybody got in there — and then we have a Somali gang problem," the career law enforcement officer told Fox News Digital. Nagel, who spent 30 years as a state trooper, claims the issue extends beyond Somali gangs, noting: "We have Somali gangs, we have Asian gangs, we have Black gangs, we have Latino gangs, and we need a gang task force." AMY KLOBUCHAR CALLS FOR MAJOR ANTI-TERRORISM INVESTMENTS AFTER ALLEGED MALL OF AMERICA PLOT The FBI thwarted a terror attack at the Mall of America, located in the Minneapolis suburb of Bloomington, on Oct. 7, 2026. Sheikhdoon Abdullahi Mohamud, 18, was arrested and charged with knowingly receiving a firearm and ammunition while knowing or having reasonable cause to believe they would be used to commit a felony and federal crime of terrorism. He is an American citizen born to Somali parents, who allegedly pledged allegiance to Somali-based ISIS offshoot al-Shabaab. Separately, Somali gangs were blamed by local officials for two separate shooting instances in the Minneapolis suburbs in past weeks. One was a mass shooting at Eden Prairie High School during the school's homecoming celebration. The shooting, which injured two, occurred in the parking lot of the high school after gang members were seen making gang signs at one another. Abdirahman Ahmed Jama, 18, was arrested on a riot charge in that incident. 100-SHOT SOMALI GANG GUN BATTLE ROCKS MINNESOTA AS SHERIFF WARNS 'WE'RE IN TROUBLE' Court documents said that Jama was the target of a later Somali gang shooting at a gas station in the town of Bloomington, likely in retaliation for the homecoming shooting, according to FOX 9. More than 100 rounds of ammunition were fired in that incident. "They don't necessarily deal in drugs yet. They're kind of a low-level gang, but they're still vicious," Nagel said of the gangs. "Primarily, they deal in guns. They buy and sell guns, illicit guns. They're also the ones that know how to take and remove some parts and basically turn a pistol into a little mini machine gun. That's what we saw in Bloomington and Eden Prairie, you know, where all of those rounds were expanded." MINNESOTA SENATE HOPEFUL WARNS THREAT LEVEL RISING AMID RASH OF SOMALI GANG CRIME, TERROR PLOT After the recent uptick in suburban Somali violence, according to Nagel, local officials have finally recognized the violence as Somali gang-related, after strong pushback from anyone who suggested that in recent years. Nagel said that when Ramsey County Sheriff Bob Fletcher said a year ago that Somali gang violence was a problem, he was called a "racist" and "immediately attacked by the Somali community." "And of course, you know, the media loves that, and they went right along with it," he said. "[The] problem was, he was right. There was a Somali gang problem." "So, we're in a really good spot because we've now all come out and said, 'Yes, we have a Somali gang problem,' and that being called a racist doesn't have a sting to it anymore," Nagel continued. FEDERAL AGENTS RAID ILHAN OMAR’S DC HOME AMID IMMIGRATION FRAUD INVESTIGATION As for Omar, who is under criminal probe for potentially falsifying information on her immigration paperwork, Nagel said she deserves due process, but that she actively tries to undermine the United States. "It's a very serious accusation, and we definitely want due process," he said. "She deserves the same investigation that everybody else would have, and in her own words, no one is above the law." REP ILHAN OMAR'S IMMIGRATION HISTORY FACES NEW SCRUTINY AS FEDERAL INVESTIGATORS SUBPOENA RELATIVES Nagel added that while it's not incumbent upon Omar to prove her innocence, he thinks it would be simple for the Somali-born congresswoman to clear up any public misunderstandings of her immigration status. "However, it would be very simple if you are innocent to be able to come up with the paperwork, do the DNA sample. I mean, there are a lot of things that you could do that put a lot this behind you, and I would think that as a politician, you know, you're not a private person anymore, you're a public person," he said. "The people that voted for you have a right to know if they can trust you, and as a politician, I would be doing everything I could to make sure that I maintain that trust. And right now, I don't see much trust in what she's doing." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Ultimately, Nagel thinks Omar views herself as a Somali first. "Her first love is Somalia. She constantly tells people that. She constantly tells the United States how we're doing everything wrong, and she constantly tries to take the United States and weaken it. "So yes, as far as I'm concerned, Somalia comes first in her life, and we are nothing more than a piggy bank for her."

articles.title: The Memo: Trump faces massive midterm rebuke — if the polls are right
articles.summary: President Trump looks to be facing a major rebuke from voters as the clock ticks down to the midterm elections. Yet, even as Democratic hopes rise, there are also nagging fears within the opposition party about its chances of taking the Senate, in particular. The overall dynamics are plainly bad for Trump and his party.…
articles.body:
President Trump looks to be facing a major rebuke from voters as the clock ticks down to the midterm elections.

Yet, even as Democratic hopes rise, there are also nagging fears within the opposition party about its chances of taking the Senate, in particular.

The overall dynamics are plainly bad for Trump and his party. The president is mired in low approval ratings. Elevated gas prices, an unpopular war and Trump’s personal penchant for controversies — and questionable construction projects — weigh him down.

Trump’s job approval rating is 20 points in negative territory according to the average maintained by The Hill’s data and polling partner, Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ). According to that metric, roughly 39 percent of Americans approve of how Trump is doing his job, while 59 percent disapprove.

The final stretch of the campaign has seen Trump campaign in states usually considered Republican strongholds, including Mississippi, South Carolina and Texas. Those rally locations speak to the reality — widely accepted within both parties — that the Senate map has expanded in the Democrats’ favor.

It’s a startling shift from the aftermath of Trump’s 2024 presidential victory when the general consensus was that the Senate would not even be in play this year, given the red-tinged nature of many of the key states.

As for the House, few political insiders expect anything other than a Democratic victory.

“The House is almost certainly going to go Democratic,” admitted GOP strategist Dan Judy. “The question is, is it a huge wave or more of a pretty solid victory?”

Regarding the upper chamber, Judy added, “It’s amazing that the Senate is even a conversation. That’s a testament to how tough an environment it is for Republicans, even by historic midterms standards.”

Trump has often noted that the party that holds the White House almost always loses seats in midterms. The sole exception this century came in the 2002 midterms, which took place against the traumatic backdrop of the 9/11 attacks the previous year.

DDHQ currently gives the Democrats an 80 percent probability of taking the House majority and a 58 percent chance of winning the Senate.

The closeness of the Senate races in some usually reliable GOP states tells its own story. A New York Times/Siena University poll released Wednesday sent shockwaves through the political world when it indicated that the race in South Carolina between Republican Sen. Darline Graham and Democrat Annie Andrews is essentially tied.

Graham was appointed to the seat this summer after the sudden death of her brother, Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.), who had been in the Senate for almost a quarter century. In the 2024 presidential contest, Trump defeated Democratic nominee Kamala Harris in South Carolina by almost 18 points.

Roughly similar stories are seen elsewhere in the nation. In Texas, Democratic nominee James Talarico leads GOP nominee Ken Paxton by 4.2 points in the DDHQ average.

In North Carolina, Democratic former Gov. Roy Cooper is widely expected to take a seat away from the GOP given his large polling advantage over Republican nominee Michael Whatley. Another political veteran, former Sen. Sherrod Brown (D), is favored by roughly 3 points in the DDHQ average as he seeks to oust Sen. Jon Husted (R) in Ohio. Trump carried Ohio by 11 points in 2024.

Yet, even amid such apparently bullish signs for the Democrats, there are plenty of nerves among the opposition party.

One fear centers on the idea that polls are decreasing in reliability for a host of reasons, including a perception that some conservative-leaning demographic groups are becoming less willing to complete surveys.

Democrats are also aware that they do not have a massive margin for error. For example, few strategists would be shocked if Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine) were to hold on to her seat, despite polls showing her down an average of about 3 points.

Talarico’s lead in Texas is eyed tentatively by Democrats who know how often their hopes have been dashed in statewide races in the Lone Star State. In Michigan, there is plenty of Democratic anxiety about Abdul El-Sayed, even though he is up 3 points in the DDHQ average. El-Sayed is attempting to retain a seat Democrats already hold, where Sen. Gary Peters (D) is retiring.

If the Democrats were to lose Michigan and fail to gain either Maine or Texas — none of which is implausible — the path to a Senate majority would suddenly seem a lot tighter.

There’s also the money factor. The New York Times recently noted that GOP ad spending is comfortably outpacing Democratic spending in six of the seven Senate races it considers toss-ups.

Democratic strategist Mark Longabaugh said that it was a combination of lack of faith in polling and “the spending disparity” that gives him restless nights.

“They seem to have unlimited money,” he said of the GOP. “In some races, we are getting outspent badly at the close of the race. In most of the races, they are not focusing on making an economic argument, they are just trying to character-smear the Democratic candidate. But I don’t underestimate their ability.”

For all that, Longabaugh pronounced himself “optimistic” overall because he believes economic discontent has left the electorate primed to exact their frustrations on Trump’s party.

Another Democratic strategist, Joe Trippi, was even more confident of his party’s chances.

Trippi argued that some of the most aggressive attacks leveled against Democratic candidates were evidence that the president and his party are having difficulty motivating their base voters.

“I think all this ‘Muslim, socialist, communist’ stuff — and Trump’s ‘Pretend I am on the ballot’ — just shows they are still grappling with how they are going to get their people to turn out,” Trippi said. “And no matter which enemy or scary thing they say is hiding under your bed, nobody is running to vote for them.”

Trippi noted that he did not expect 2024 MAGA voters to back Democrats in any significant number this time around.

But, he said, the reluctance of those voters to back the GOP — citing living costs, the war on Iran and Trump’s propensity for self-glorifying projects, among other factors — was clear.

The Memo is a reported column by Niall Stanage.

articles.title: Democrats eye ways to rein in the power of future presidents
articles.summary: Confident in their odds of flipping the House, Democrats are eyeing ways to curb the powers of the presidency. The effort is not likely to result in any significant reforms while President Trump remains in office and controls the veto pen. But Democrats, who have long accused Trump of abusing his executive authority, want to…
articles.body:
Confident in their odds of flipping the House, Democrats are eyeing ways to curb the powers of the presidency.

The effort is not likely to result in any significant reforms while President Trump remains in office and controls the veto pen. But Democrats, who have long accused Trump of abusing his executive authority, want to send the message that the country needs robust new guardrails to ensure future presidents don’t follow Trump’s playbook.

“This administration has revealed the holes in our checks and balances, and it’s very clear that power has swung way too far in the direction of the executive branch, and the abuses of norms point out that perhaps we need to codify some of these norms,” Rep. Suhas Subramanyam (D-Va.) said.

“It baffles me that the president continues to openly defy Congress as well, and our recourse involves hoping that the executive branch agencies like the DOH [Department of Justice] will enforce some of our powers when it’s very clear that those agencies are now simply loyalists to the president, so there’s generally a lot we need to do to patch some of the holes in our system,” he added.

The push is reminiscent of the effort at the end of Trump’s first term, when Democrats controlled the House gavels and were widely critical of his expansive view of presidential power — not least Trump’s efforts to use the office to overturn the results of his 2020 election defeat.

The violence of Jan. 6, 2021, led to Trump’s second impeachment and stirred a sense that his political career was over. Since voters reelected Trump to the White House in 2024, however, he has only been more aggressive in exerting executive powers , using the office to pardon people convicted of violent crimes , gut the federal workforce and prosecute perceived political enemies .

Those moves have infuriated Democrats and renewed the appetite within the party to move legislation designed to rein in the actions they deem to be abusive. Some see it as a Watergate moment, when Congress passed a number of laws designed to curb presidential power in the wake of former President Nixon’s ignominious fall.

“I think what we’ve learned with this Trump administration is they’ve pushed the envelope, gone beyond the envelope in so many ways … we should know that we need to significantly tighten that up and codify things in the law that we just had assumed, our previous Congresses had assumed, administrations wouldn’t try to do,” Rep. James Walkinshaw (D-Va.) said.

One reform Democrats are targeting is increasing transparency around presidential pardon power. The issue had drawn renewed scrutiny after Trump had issued sweeping pardons to hundreds of people charged with crimes tied to the Jan. 6 Capitol attack.

Former President Biden also pardoned his son Hunter Biden in 2024, which quickly infuriated Republicans. Hunter Biden had pleaded guilty to nine federal tax charges and was found guilty on three felony charges over his purchase and possession of a gun in 2018.

“We need to make sure that any criminal history of a pardon recipient is made very public, and we can prevent individuals who receive a presidential pardon from making a large contribution to the president or his party, as well as to the president’s family or friends,” Subramanyam said.

“Part of the issue is pardons are essentially for sale now. We have lobbyists going around trying to sell their pardon power by saying, ‘If you pay me X amount, I’ll go get you a pardon, and then just throw this much money into a campaign committee,’ or maybe, ‘Do this deal with the president’s family, and we can pardon you,’” Subramanyam said.

Subramanyam introduced legislation , dubbed the No Pardon Paydays Act, in September with Democratic Reps. Ted Lieu (Calif.) and Joe Neguse (Colo.) that would require the pardon attorney to “submit a review to Congress” of any pardon recipient’s criminal history. It would also bar such recipients from making high-end donations to political action committees tied to the president who issued the pardon.

Democrats are also keen to curb the president’s powers to fire federal workers. That purge was a major component of Trump’s first year back in office, when he formed the Department of Government Efficiency, led by Elon Musk, to slash the federal workforce in the name of cutting federal spending and weeding out “deep state” bureaucrats.

The firings have been challenged in the courts — in some cases successfully — but not before thousands of federal employees had already retired or moved into jobs outside of government. The issue resonates with particular intensity for Democrats in the Washington area, who represent a disproportionate number of federal workers and want to protect those constituents going forward.

Walkinshaw said he plans to reintroduce legislation, dubbed the Limit on Sweeping Executive Reorganization Act, in January. His bill requires “any proposed reorganization that cuts large numbers of federal employees, slashes budgets, or outsources core government functions to secure explicit approval from Congress,” according to a press release .

“Obviously, that’s in response to what we’ve seen with USAID [U.S. Agency for International Development] being dismantled, Department of Education being dismantled, CFPB [Consumer Financial Protection Bureau] being effectively shut down. So I think it would reestablish the balance between the president’s constitutional authority to manage the federal government as the executive with Congress’s power of the purse and right to establish and fund federal agencies,” Walkinshaw said.

Democrats are also hoping to reinforce Congress’s power of the purse and ensure that funds appropriated by lawmakers are spent as directed. This comes as the Trump administration has faced scrutiny over its efforts to withhold congressionally approved funding .

The Government Accountability Office, for instance, found that the Department of Health and Human Services withheld more than $78 million in research grant funding in fiscal 2025, violating the Impoundment Control Act.

Trump also redirected millions of dollars meant to go to the U.S. National Park Service to D.C.-based projects.

“The ads that he aired during the World Series and playoff games, paid for by the U.S. government. Where’s that money coming from?” Rep. Dave Min (D-Calif.) said. “Because it wasn’t from Congress.”

“He’s taking money from elsewhere and reappropriating, same as he did with … the White House ballroom, the reflecting pool, all these pet projects,” he added. “He’s taking money that we appropriated for certain purposes and using it for his own purposes. That’s totally illegal. The problem again is no one’s enforcing the law.”

Min, along with Democratic Reps. Eugene Vindman (Va.) and Sam Liccardo (Calif.), introduced a bill last year that would allow individuals, states and local jurisdictions to challenge the administration’s impoundment of funds.

Trump’s return to office has been accompanied by a massive increase in his personal wealth, from $2.4 billion in 2024 to roughly $6.6 billion today, according to Forbes .

The president says he’s benefited from a robust economy, particularly the surging stock market. But some of those gains have come from his meme coin and other cryptocurrency ventures controlled by his family, which has profited from the industry even as Trump has relaxed regulations governing it.

Democrats are vowing to tighten the screws. They’ve already introduced numerous bills to restrict presidents from using the office for personal gain, including legislation prohibiting the commander in chief from suing his administration to secure a financial settlement , as Trump did with the Internal Revenue Service earlier this year.

Democrats are also likely to move legislation barring federal policymakers from owning and trading individual stocks. House Republicans had passed one version of that bill this year, but it was opposed by most Democrats because Trump was exempt from the restrictions. The Democrats’ alternative bill would include presidents and vice presidents.

“We need to put the best legislation forward that protects the American people and reins in corruption and abuse, and put it on the president’s desk,” Subramanyam said. “If he decides he wants to veto a bill that will rein in corruption, then he’s on the record as doing that.”

“What I found is when we put good legislation on the president’s desk that has overwhelming support from the public, he often gets cornered into either signing it or just letting it go into law without signing it directly, instead of vetoing it,” he continued. “So we need to make sure that we put the best legislation on his desk and force him into a hard decision whether to veto popular legislation.”

Still, Rep. Mark Pocan (D-Wis.) said Democrats will focus on ensuring existing laws are properly enforced, noting that new legislation “doesn’t necessarily” have to be passed to rein in some of the administration’s actions.

“Most of [Trump’s] actions have been illegal, so the easiest way to address them isn’t trying to pass a new law to get through the House and the Senate and have signed by the guy that you’re going against,” Pocan said.

“It’s going to be going through the courts and enforcing current law,” he added. “And then secondly, we can try to introduce legislation to make people aware of things. But you know, do we think Donald Trump’s going to sign them into law? Less likely, so we’re going to be doing things the most effective way.”

articles.title: Democrats see battleground map expand to South Carolina, Florida, Mississippi
articles.summary: Democrats are giddy about the possibility of a bigger blue wave than expected in the battle for the Senate as polls show that South Carolina, Florida and Mississippi — three seats that were long seen as safe Republican holds — are now competitive races. Democrats view the Republican candidates running in those states as mediocre political…
articles.body:
Democrats are giddy about the possibility of a bigger blue wave than expected in the battle for the Senate as polls show that South Carolina , Florida and Mississippi — three seats that were long seen as safe Republican holds — are now competitive races.

Democrats view the Republican candidates running in those states as mediocre political talents who must fight historic headwinds caused by President Trump’s unpopularity, voter anger over inflation and the war in Iran, and burgeoning Democratic voter enthusiasm.

The Senate battleground map has steadily expanded throughout the 2026 midterm election cycle as political handicappers have shifted seats that were thought to be in solidly Republican territory — such as Alaska, Iowa, Kansas and Texas — to the “toss-up” category.

But now Republicans have to worry about losing Senate seats in states that were unthinkable as realistic Democratic pickup opportunities at the start of the election cycle, most notably South Carolina, which last elected a Democrat, Fritz Hollings, to the Senate in 1998.

A New York Times/Siena poll of 707 voters in South Carolina published Wednesday showed Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.) tied with Democrat Annie Andrews, 48 percent to 48 percent.

The poll showed Andrews with support from 57 percent of independent voters and 7 percent of Republican voters.

“Everybody’s got to understand that this could be a monumental election, that the normal arithmetic of voting adds up differently,” said Tad Devine, a Democratic strategist who worked on several presidential campaigns.

“The way Democrats can win — and South Carolina can be a great example — all through the South is to have a multiracial coalition that relies on overwhelming support of African American voters and solid support from white voters,” he said, citing former President Biden’s and Democratic Sens. Jon Ossoff’s and Raphael Warnock’s victories in Georgia in 2020.

Democrats knocked off two GOP incumbents in Georgia that year, and Biden narrowly defeated Trump in the state.

Devine noted Biden won Georgia with a sizeable minority of white voters at 27 percent, according to an estimate by The New York Times, and an overwhelming majority of Black voters at 92 percent.

Devine said Biden had won more than 30 percent of white voters in Georgia, a number that is difficult to gauge because it relies on exit polling and other imprecise measurements. And he said that Ossoff and Warnock won with similar percentages of white voters.

Democrats think a similar formula of a larger-than-usual number of white Southern voters casting ballots for their candidates and big turnout from minority voters in favor of their party could produce victories next week in unexpected places, such as South Carolina, Texas and even Florida and Mississippi.

The nonpartisan Cook Political Report rates South Carolina as having a partisan lean of R+8, which measures the leaning of a state in a neutral environment. It rates Texas as R+6, Florida as R+, and Mississippi as R+11.

“These coalitions — if you put them together state by state and you have a target — mean that Democrats can win statewide races in places like South Carolina, Georgia, really across the board. We’ll see whether or not it works in Mississippi, too,” Devine said.

“I think it’s all possible this year because Trump has changed the calculus, and he’s really gone in and taken groups of voters who were reliably Republican and turned them into swing voters,” he continued. “I would not be surprised to see any of these long-shot races come home for Democrats next Tuesday.”

The New York Times/Siena poll found only 42 percent of likely voters in South Carolina strongly or somewhat approve of Trump’s job performance while 55 percent disapprove.

White voters made up 71 percent of registered voters in South Carolina in 2024 and Black voters made up 24 percent, according to a report from the South Carolina Election Commission.

Senate Republicans argue that pollsters, especially those working for legacy media outlets and universities, have a long track record of overestimating the strength of Democratic candidates in GOP-leaning states such as South Carolina and Texas.

“The polling industry is blowing the whistle on its own negligence and track record of misses in Senate races,” said Bernadette Breslin, the national press secretary for the National Republican Senatorial Committee (NRSC).

“Senate Republicans remain focused on exposing Democrats’ dangerous, unaffordable agenda while racking up historic victories that have helped level the playing field on spending and put [Senate Minority Leader] Chuck Schumer [(D-N.Y.)] on defense,” she continued.

Breslin noted Owen Winter, a reporter for The Economist, observed that if polling errors follow the average historical trend, the leads that Democratic Senate candidates have in Alaska and Texas could be “wiped out,” and toss-up races in Iowa and Kansas would move “firmly into the Republican column.”

The Cook Political Report rates South Carolina as “lean” Republican, Mississippi as “likely” Republican and Florida as “solid” Republican.

A New York Times/Siena survey of 813 voters in Florida, also released Wednesday, showed Democrat Angie Nixon trailing Republican incumbent Sen. Ashley Moody by 6 percentage points — 44 percent to 50 percent.

Democrats in Washington have largely ignored the Florida Senate race but some in the party think that a surprise in the Sunshine State is not out of the question.

“Notwithstanding what’s happened in Florida in recent years, I’ve always believed Florida is a place where Democrats with the right candidate and the right message can put together a winning coalition,” Devine said. “And I’ve seen that going way back, I worked for [former Sen.] Bill Nelson [(D-Fla.)] when he was insurance commissioner and also in the first couple of Senate races that he did there that he won.”

He said that Black voter turnout “skyrocketed” in the 2000 presidential election, which put then-Vice President Al Gore within several hundred votes of winning the state.

Black voters made up 12 percent of the general election electorate in Florida in 2024.

Trump won Florida over former Vice President Kamala Harris by more than 13 percentage points two years ago even though Harris won an estimated 35 percent of white voters.

But Trump was able to run up a large margin of victory in large part because he won 13 percent of Black voters and a whopping 56 percent of Hispanic voters.

Democratic strategists believe Hispanic voters will shift decisively toward Democratic candidates, driven by Trump’s lower approval ratings on handling the economy, inflation and immigration enforcement.

Steve Jarding, a Democratic strategist who previously worked as a senior adviser to the Senate Democrats’ campaign arm, agreed that South Carolina and other Republican-leaning states are on the table.

He said that Democrats in South Carolina “are performing like a +11 or +12,” putting Graham’s Senate race in play. He said Florida could also be in striking distance for Democrats.

“It’s going be contingent on turnout. Democrats seem to be fired up, Republicans less so,” he said.

Jarding noted that Democrats have won by healthy margins in special election races since Trump took office in 2025, saying, “All of a sudden a R+8 state is in play.”

“There could be a hell of a lot of states in play,” he said. “Florida would be interesting to me.”

“I’d be more surprised with Florida, I would not be surprised with South Carolina,” Jarding added.

The New York Times/Siena survey found only 43 percent of Florida voters approve of Trump’s job performance while 53 percent disapprove.

Democratic strategists think that young voters — who turned out in huge numbers in the 2008 presidential election, helping former President Obama win in Republican-leanings states such as Indiana and North Carolina — could be a wild-card factor in next week’s election.

Democrats also gained seven Senate seats in 2008 — not counting the Minnesota race which was subject to an extended recount.

Democrats are quietly hoping that the Mississippi Senate race, where low-profile Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith is running for reelection, could be another election night surprise.

The Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee made a splash this week by announcing a $500,000 coordinated ad buy with Mississippi Democratic Senate candidate Scott Colom. Semafor first reported the coordinated ad buy Thursday.

Democrats have pounced on Hyde-Smith’s awkward response earlier this year when asked about skyrocketing beef prices. Hyde-Smith, who usually refuses to talk to reporters in the Senate hallways, inartfully pointed out “you have so many proteins to choose from” if you can’t afford steaks or hamburgers.

A Change Research poll of 842 likely Mississippi voters conducted from Oct. 21-22 and sponsored by the Democratic-aligned Government That Works PAC found Hyde-Smith leading Colom by only 3 percentage points, 43 percent to 40 percent.

Breslin, the NRSC’s national press secretary, slammed Colom for being supported by progressive megadonor George Soros.

“Instead of saving himself the embarrassment of being denied a job twice by Hyde-Smith, Colom is running a campaign backed by Chuck Schumer, funded by George Soros, and built on pro-transgender and other far-left policies,” she said.

Hyde-Smith blocked Colom’s nomination to serve as a federal judge during the Biden administration.

articles.title: Trump faces ‘purest referendum’ in South Carolina
articles.summary: South Carolina’s surprisingly competitive Senate race poses one of the clearest tests of President Trump’s continued sway over Republican voters, as his popularity sinks across the political spectrum. He’ll return to the state for the second time in two weeks Thursday, seeking to boost South Carolina Sen. Darline Graham (R), who he backed in a…
articles.body:
South Carolina’s surprisingly competitive Senate race poses one of the clearest tests of President Trump’s continued sway over Republican voters, as his popularity sinks across the political spectrum.

He’ll return to the state for the second time in two weeks Thursday, seeking to boost South Carolina Sen. Darline Graham (R), who he backed in a bruising primary fight to replace her late brother Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.).

A New York Times/Siena poll released Wednesday showed Graham and her Democratic opponent Annie Andrews neck and neck in the state that Trump won by 17 points two years ago.

“Trump helps a lot. More than a lot. He is everything in this race. But for him nobody outside her immediate family would know who Darline is,” said one high-ranking South Carolina Republican.

“That said, that makes this election perhaps the purest referendum on Trump we’ve seen to date. More so than even [Ken] Paxton or Herschel Walker,” the Republican added.

Trump’s upcoming visit to Rock Hill, S.C., will also put him squarely in the backyard of Graham’s chief primary rival, Rep. Ralph Norman (R-S.C.).

Norman, who has broken with Trump numerous times in the past, told CNN on Tuesday that the Senate race is an attempt to “force” a candidate onto South Carolina voters.

“The voters in South Carolina are not buying the argument that everyone has to ‘settle’ for a candidate that has been propped up by special interest groups and a Republican president spending millions of dollars spreading false narratives about why Darline Graham is qualified to be elected to the U.S. Senate for the next six years,” the congressman said Tuesday.

Graham defeated Norman in the state’s Republican primary runoff in August by just under 5 points. Maggie Knox, a South Carolina GOP official, predicted that the fallout of Norman’s criticism of Graham would not impact her support with the conservative base by more than 1 percent on Election Day.

“What I see is a lot of noise from folks who are not involved, who are not in leadership positions, who are not influential anymore saying, ‘Write in Ralph,’ but I just don’t think that’s going to happen,” said Tyson Grinstead, chair of South Carolina’s Richland County Republican Party and former Sen. Lindsey Graham campaign adviser.

Knox said a bigger concern is whether Republicans feel motivated to vote at all.

“Complacency is our greatest enemy right now,” she said.

Rock Hill is also strategically located along the North Carolina border, giving Graham earned media in the expensive Charlotte media market and allowing Trump to boost North Carolina Senate candidate Michael Whatley (R).

“It’s not really so much that he’s focusing on South Carolina super hard, but I think that [he’s] once again helping us fight complacency, but certainly making sure North Carolinians show up,” Knox said.

However, Trump’s popularity across the country, including in the Carolinas, has taken a hit as a result of the economy and the Iran war. According to a Civiqs tracking poll, Trump’s approval rating in the Palmetto State sits at 41 percent while his disapproval rating clocks in at 51 percent.

Whatley, another hand-picked Trump candidate, is widely expected to lose to the popular former Gov. Roy Cooper (D) in North Carolina’s Senate race.

And as Trump’s popularity continues to decline, Senate Republicans have faced closer-than-expected races in what are normally considered reliably red states, including South Carolina.

Wednesday’s New York Times/Siena poll showed Graham and Andrews tied at 48 percent with a margin of error of 4.3 percent. Meanwhile, a poll released by The Citadel on Tuesday showed Graham with a 4-point lead over Andrews, and a South Carolina Policy Center poll released on the same day showed Graham up by 2 points.

Last week, the nonpartisan Cook Political Report moved the race toward Democrats, from “likely Republican” to “lean Republican.”

South Carolina Democratic strategist Antjuan Seawright predicted Trump’s visits to the state will be “a base motivator” — for Democrats.

“I honestly think the race is a 50-50 jump ball,” Seawright said. “For Democrats, we must get down the field every time we have the ball in our hands, and the ball is in our hands at this point.”

This week, Andrews received a joint, bipartisan endorsement from former South Carolina Govs. David Beasley (R) and Jim Hodges (D). Beasley lost his reelection bid to Hodges, the last Democratic governor of the state, in 1998.

Beasley has become an outspoken critic of the GOP and wrote in an op-ed last week that the party “is not the party that I consider myself a member of.”

Democrats also note Andrews’s recent efforts to target Republican and independent voters in red-leaning areas of the state, including Aiken County, where she held a town hall earlier this week. Andrews has also made stops in Myrtle Beach, Little River, Fort Mill, Union, Camden, Anderson, Lancaster and Lyman.

Fort Mill, Union, Camden and Lancaster are all located in Norman’s district.

Graham will also campaign in Norman’s district when Trump hits the campaign in Rock Hill. The visit comes as Norman has lashed out at Graham and Trump in the final days before the election.

In an interview with CNN on Wednesday, Rep. Nancy Mace (R-S.C.) predicted that Graham will “barely” pull it off but acknowledged the impact of the resistance of some in the conservative base to Graham.

“There is an effort afoot where people are pushing back on this narrative where they’re going to be shoved a candidate down our throat to vote a certain way. I think that people feel boondoggled,” Mace said.

articles.title: Johnson signals he’ll remain atop GOP, scrambling leadership landscape
articles.summary: Speaker Mike Johnson’s (R-La.) recent hints that he intends to remain GOP leader even if Republicans lose the House have rattled the party’s leadership outlook and raised fresh new questions about the GOP’s future heading into the next Congress. Most House Speakers in recent decades have stepped out of Congress after losing the gavel. And…
articles.body:
Speaker Mike Johnson’s (R-La.) recent hints that he intends to remain GOP leader even if Republicans lose the House have rattled the party’s leadership outlook and raised fresh new questions about the GOP’s future heading into the next Congress.

Most House Speakers in recent decades have stepped out of Congress after losing the gavel. And Reps. Steve Scalise (R-La.), the majority leader, and Jim Jordan (R-Ohio), a conservative icon, are both expected to launch bids to lead House Republicans if Democrats flip the chamber, according to GOP lawmakers, aides and strategists.

But Johnson recently muddled the leadership landscape by signaling his intention to keep his spot atop the party even if Republicans are knocked out of power. Then on Monday, President Trump offered a glowing endorsement of Johnson’s leadership chops, sparking further speculation that Johnson might, in fact, buck historic trends and try to remain leader even from the minority.

“Mike Johnson is a true friend, fighter, and WINNER,” Trump posted on his social media account, “and he has my Complete and Total endorsement for Re-Election.”

“Thank you, President @realDonaldTrump!” Johnson responded. “The best is yet to come as we save America!”

Much about the leadership race is expected to come into sharper focus after next Tuesday’s midterm elections. A Johnson spokesman said the Speaker is “solely focused on protecting the majority,” noting that he “will campaign in 21 districts across 13 states between now and Election Day.”

But many Republicans are skeptical, predicting that Johnson will follow the example of past GOP Speakers — including Newt Gingrich (Ga.), Dennis Hastert (Ill.), Paul Ryan (Wis.) and Kevin McCarthy (Calif.) — who all left Capitol Hill in short order after losing the gavel.

“I highly doubt that the Speaker will go for minority leader at this point,” a GOP aide said Wednesday. “I just don’t see him having a desire. I don’t think he’s having a fun time as Speaker. I don’t think he’d want to be minority leader.”

Former Speaker Nancy Pelosi (D-Calif.) defied modern tradition in 2011, when she clung to the minority leader seat after the party was clobbered in the 2010 midterms. Pelosi would win the gavel back eight years later, but she’s been the exception.

GOP strategist Amy Frederiksen said that “when you lose, and you’re no longer Speaker…it’s hard to go back to minority leader.”

“There’s certainly a lot less trappings and a lot less power, and also the caucus just tends to kind of want to clean some house. Like members just see it as an opportunity to just switch things up, and so it’s not that it hasn’t happened, of course. Speaker Pelosi went to be the minority leader, so it isn’t unprecedented,” Frederiksen said. “It wouldn’t be historic in any kind of way, and it’s very possible. But it is — I don’t think it’s as simple as him just deciding. I think that the caucus is going to really want to weigh in on things.”

She added that Johnson was a “compromise candidate anyway” for Speaker.

“We went through a couple, two, three, four different potential speakers, including Steve Scalise and Jim Jordan, when he was finally chosen as Speaker, so I, you know, I just think that there is that,” she said. “It was sort of a bargain struck anyway for him to be Speaker.”

Some Republicans predicted next year’s leadership roster will hinge on how, exactly, the midterms play out. Although Trump is not on the ballot, the elections are shaping up to be a referendum on the president, whose historic unpopularity has created huge challenges for GOP candidates and made Democrats the favorite to control the House next year.

Still, some Republicans believe that if Democrats win by a wide margin, Johnson will bear much of the blame, lose support within the conference and struggle to secure the votes needed to become minority leader, even if Trump wanted him there.

“I would imagine there to be more of a push for someone else, just given that over, you know, a billion dollars has been spent on the midterms alone,” a second GOP staffer, who spoke on the condition of anonymity, told The Hill earlier this month.

Although both Scalise and Jordan have downplayed their interest in the top spot, many Republicans say they’re both angling for the position, setting the stage for a potentially messy internal fight when House lawmakers return to Washington the week after the midterms. (Minnesota Rep. Tom Emmer, the Republican whip, says he wants to remain in that seat).

There’s plenty of disagreement about who has the advantage in such a race. Some say that if it’s a two-way race between Scalise and Jordan, Scalise would likely be better positioned than Jordan to step into the top spot given his current leadership position.

“I think for Scalise… it’d be an easy transition for him to step into that. But for Jordan, he’s really — how do I phrase this? He’s been a loyal soldier. He’s rallied people well, and he’s an effective politician. So I think both would do well in the role, but I think Scalise would have an easier transition just out of pure — his House leadership currently,” a third GOP staffer said.

The first Republican staffer, though, predicted Jordan has the edge.

“He’s done a lot of work over the past couple years where he’s kind of built his own coalition, [and] he does have, like, a cult following around the country when he goes on the campaign trail. So I do think it’s his to lose at this point,” the first aide said. “When you’re in the minority, you need somebody who can be a fighter and willing to go out there and go on TV and bomb some bombs. And I think he’s the guy for it.”

The offices of Scalise and Jordan did not respond to requests for comment on Wednesday.

Johnson has faced a rocky tenure as Speaker, often marked by internal GOP fighting, a razor-thin margin and repeated challenges in keeping his conference united on government spending, the Iran war and other issues.

Even so, Johnson told CBS News’s Robert Costa this month that in the “unlikely scenario” Republicans lose the House, “I would expect my colleagues would ask me to continue leading this conference, even if we have divided government.”

“I’m going to continue to serve my highest best use to God and country, and I believe right now, as we’re sitting here, that’s the Speaker of the House,” Johnson said. “And if we lost the majority, I don’t think that that position that I have would change. I think I would stay right there.”

Some Republicans note that if Johnson were to jump in the minority leader race, he would have a strong case for the position.

The third GOP staffer noted that Johnson’s “had to deal with a lot of curveballs,” and that he’s handled them well.

“I think that the party recognizes that and will react accordingly,” the staffer said. “That doesn’t mean there’s not people gunning for the same spot, but I think Johnson has been a good leader, a team player amidst what is you know — we could say honestly — has been some chaos at times.”

articles.title: America's enemies prepare to take the next major war into outer space
articles.summary: China and Russia are developing anti-satellite weapons including lasers, orbital interceptors and a nuclear space weapon that could cripple U.S. forces.
articles.body: The opening moves of the next major war could unfold hundreds of miles above Earth. U.S. adversaries are looking at ways to blind American forces in future conflict by jamming communications, disabling GPS, using lasers to attack satellites or destroying them completely. A sweeping new Defense Intelligence Agency assessment details how China and Russia are developing sophisticated ways to disrupt or destroy U.S. satellites. This includes a Russian satellite designed to carry a nuclear weapon into Earth's orbit. American forces rely on satellites to communicate across battlefields, navigate ships and aircraft, track enemy forces, detect missile launches and guide precision weapons to their targets. Knocking those systems offline could leave forces below struggling to see, communicate and strike. AMERICA'S NEXT WAR COULD REACH US SOIL, TOP ARMY GENERAL WARNS "We can't do military operations the way that we do them today without satellites, without systems in space," Clayton Swope, deputy director of the Aerospace Security Project at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, previously told Fox News Digital. "Whoever has space and can deny that to their adversary has a huge asymmetric advantage in a conflict," Swope said. CHINA IS TAKING THE FIGHT TO THE STARS. AMERICA MUST RECLAIM SPACE SUPREMACY Beyond the battlefield, satellites underpin everything from GPS navigation and communications to banking, transportation and the electric grid, meaning a large-scale attack in space could disrupt services millions of people rely on every day. Chinese military thinkers have identified reconnaissance, communications, navigation and early-warning satellites as potential targets for attacks designed to "blind and deafen the enemy," according to the report. DIA assesses Beijing could begin threatening or gradually degrading an adversary’s space architecture during a crisis as a "prelude to war." Russia, meanwhile, views U.S. reliance on satellites for precision strikes and projecting military power as a "critical vulnerability" to exploit during a conflict. Its doctrine envisions attacks ranging from temporary jamming and blinding satellite sensors to the outright destruction of spacecraft and the infrastructure supporting them. DIA describes the threat as a continuum, beginning with attacks that can temporarily disrupt a satellite without destroying it and escalating through cyber and orbital attacks to kinetic weapons and, ultimately, a nuclear detonation in space. Some of those tactics have already made their way into active conflict. During Operation Epic Fury, the U.S. and Iran "took offensive actions against each other's space capabilities to degrade and disrupt military actions on both sides," according to DIA. The report does not detail those operations, but says jamming near the Strait of Hormuz in June disrupted U.S. aircraft and shipping vessels. The Chinese military already practices jamming satellite communications and GPS during military exercises. Beijing also has ground-based lasers capable of disrupting or damaging satellites in low-Earth orbit, and DIA assesses it could field space-based directed-energy systems by the late 2020s. Other Chinese systems can get much closer. The Shijian-17 satellite has a robotic arm capable of grappling another satellite, while Shijian-21 used similar technology in 2022 to move a defunct Chinese navigation satellite into a higher orbit. DIA noted that the same technology used to service or remove satellites can also have military applications. Russia has repeatedly put its own spacecraft near U.S. satellites. Cosmos 2543 began following a U.S. national security satellite after it was released into orbit in 2019, approaching it several times before later firing a projectile in what DIA described as an anti-satellite weapons test. PENTAGON REVEALS SECRET SPACE WEAPONS ARE ALREADY IN ORBIT — BUT WON'T SAY WHAT THEY DO Russia sent Cosmos 2558 near another U.S. government satellite in 2022, and two years later launched Cosmos 2576 into the same orbit as a U.S. national security satellite before it began moving toward the American spacecraft. By 2025, Cosmos 2588 was maneuvering within roughly 93 kilometers of another U.S. government satellite. Russia is also developing Burevestnik, an air-launched weapon intended to "kill" satellites in low-Earth orbit, according to DIA. The weapon would be launched from a modified MiG-31 aircraft and could be placed into orbit with little or no warning. The threat escalates dramatically with Russia’s nuclear ambitions. "Russia is developing a satellite designed to carry a nuclear weapon," the assessment states. Such a weapon could cause the "rapid and sudden loss or degradation of thousands of satellites" operated by governments and companies around the world, disrupting communications, navigation, weather forecasting and national security systems. The damage could continue long after the initial blast. DIA warns that a nuclear detonation in space would leave behind radiation belts that "could persist for years" and damage satellites that initially survived or were only temporarily disrupted. The threat has been on Washington’s radar for years. Then-House Intelligence Committee Chairman Mike Turner set off alarm bells in February 2024 when he called on the Biden administration to declassify intelligence about a "serious national security threat," later revealed to involve a Russian nuclear anti-satellite capability. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP U.S. officials have generally been more guarded about the underlying intelligence. As recently as April, U.S. Space Command chief Gen. Stephen Whiting said officials were "very concerned" by reports that Russia was potentially considering placing a nuclear anti-satellite weapon in orbit, but declined to confirm whether Moscow was actually developing one.

articles.title: ActBlue's woes not over as top Republican predicts potential DOJ charges over foreign cash controversy
articles.summary: Top House Republican Bryan Steil warns ActBlue could face criminal charges after President Donald Trump ordered the DOJ to investigate.
articles.body: A top House Republican leading the investigation into ActBlue is warning that Democrats' main fundraising platform could potentially face criminal charges. Committee on House Administration Chairman Bryan Steil, R-Wis., told Fox News Digital that the congressional investigation into ActBlue would continue and that he suspected the Department of Justice (DOJ) would act as well if federal prosecutors believed a crime could be proven in court. "We know that ActBlue did not have the fraud prevention standards in place that were necessary to prevent foreign funds from finding their way, through the ActBlue platform, into Democratic campaigns and Democratic causes. I'm of the belief that we ultimately need to continue this investigation," Steil told Fox News Digital. ANOTHER ACTBLUE LEADER PLEADS FIFTH AS HOUSE INVESTIGATES ALLEGED FOREIGN DONATIONS "And then, separate of that, the United States Department of Justice will make a decision as to whether or not they believe that there was a crime committed. And if they can prove that in court, my belief would be that the Department of Justice would move forward." Steil's committee, along with the House committees on oversight and the judiciary, have for years probed allegations that ActBlue's lax verification standards have allowed foreign cash to seep into American elections. ActBlue has denied any wrongdoing and dismissed the probe as a partisan attack. DEM FUNDRAISING GIANT MAKES DAMNING ADMISSION AS GOP PROBES FOREIGN DONATION ALLEGATIONS ActBlue has, however, sought to shore up its donor verification standards as the probe has gone on, including most recently rolling out a new passport verification system. "Our investigation is about getting the facts to the American people, and, in large part, putting ourselves in a position to update our campaign finance laws for the digital era," Steil said. "So many of our campaign finance laws were written for a previous time. It is absolutely essential that we're updating our laws to actually address the fact that we are in a campaign finance digital era." President Donald Trump directed now-former Attorney General Pam Bondi to open an investigation into ActBlue in April 2025, but the current status of that probe is unknown. Fox News Digital reached out to the DOJ with Steil's comments, asking for an update on the investigation. The platform has long been used by many Democrats to raise money for their political campaigns, including Democratic leaders in the House and Senate, though it said it paused donations from Americans abroad in 2025. FAR-LEFT POLITICIANS STILL USING ACTBLUE AS 88-YEAR-OLD DISPUTES DONATING NEARLY $150,000 TO FUNDRAISING GIANT ActBlue has consistently denied wrongdoing in responses to Fox News Digital and communications to House investigators. Ten top figures within the company, including executives and founders, have pleaded the Fifth Amendment to avoid answering questions in both public and private sit-downs with GOP-led committees. But a new report released earlier this month, first reported by Fox News Digital, appeared to show employees green-lighting donations despite some questions about where they came from. Chief among the GOP's concerns was ActBlue's passport number verification. According to the report, the field only required the correct number of characters for a U.S. passport number rather than a valid code for a donation to be accepted. A letter sent to House investigators by ActBlue's lawyers earlier this month said its new program "adds passport-based identity verification as a further enhancement to ActBlue’s multi-layered approach to fraud and foreign-contribution prevention." TEXAS AG PAXTON SUES DEM FUNDRAISING PLATFORM ACTBLUE, ALLEGING 'FRAUDULENT AND FOREIGN DONATIONS' "The new program uses the best available technology to allow eligible donors located abroad to verify their identity using a valid U.S. passport. It reflects substantial engineering investments by ActBlue to ensure that, as it resumes processing contributions from foreign addresses, its compliance systems can withstand scrutiny," the letter said. Steil said at the time that the update "only confirms what we've been saying: ActBlue failed to verify the citizenship of individuals who made donations from abroad." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Fox News Digital reached out to ActBlue for comment on Steil's most recent remarks.

articles.title: Alaska governor orders probe into Democratic campaign's alleged links to same-name candidate
articles.summary: The Republican governor was responding to allegations in the New York Times that Democrats recruited a spoiler candidate, Dan Sullivan.
articles.body:
The Republican governor of Alaska has ordered an investigation into an alleged "scheme" which led to two Dan Sullivans standing in the state's US Senate race.

Governor Mike Dunleavy said he was responding to a New York Times (NYT) story which said the team of Democratic candidate Mary Peltola worked with people who tried to recruit spoiler candidates in the Senate race.

The governor's post on X said he would investigate "whether this scheme violated Alaska's laws". He did not say which laws he had in mind.

Dan Sullivan, the incumbent Republican senator running for re-election, and allies have accused the Democrats of trying to confuse voters. Peltola's team deny any wrongdoing.

They say they did not encourage the second Dan Sullivan, a retired teacher who lives in a remote fishing village, to stand. He has denied any links with the Peltola campaign.

The ballot paper is set to list the two men as Dan S Sullivan, who will be described as the incumbent Republican senator, and Daniel J Sullivan Jr.

Senator Dan Sullivan told Fox News on Wednesday night that Peltola should "come clean" and described it as a scandal of the highest order.

His fellow Republican senator in Alaska, Lisa Murkowksi, accused the Democratic campaign of engaging in a "pattern of lies". President Donald Trump has called for Peltola to be barred.

The Alaska race is considered by analysts to be one of the tightest of the upcoming US midterm elections, which will decide which party controls Congress. Americans head to the polls across the country on Tuesday.

Previous efforts by the Republicans to remove that Sullivan, the retired teacher, from the ballot have already been rejected by the Alaska Supreme Court which found no state laws had been broken by him running in the race.

The Trump administration filed a legal case last week aimed at preventing the certification of the result if the Trump-backed Sullivan loses, arguing that the presence of both Sullivans on the ballot could confuse voters. Some legal experts were sceptical they would have a case, given the Alaska court ruling.

But Dunleavy's statement, which did not name the Peltola campaign, said the NYT reporting had supported findings by the state Division of Elections earlier this year.

"I am therefore directing the Department of Public Safety to investigate whether this scheme violated Alaska's laws and whether criminal charges or civil action are warranted," he wrote. "The evidence will determine what happens next."

The NYT report alleged that people connected to Peltola's campaign, as well as senior aides at the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee (DSCC), worked to try to recruit Sullivan the schoolteacher to stand in the Senate race.

This was part of a broader effort to encourage other would-be "spoiler" candidates to enter the race and dilute the support of the sitting Republican senator, the newspaper reported.

The paper said it had seen text messages and interviewed 12 people who who participated in or were told of the plan, or were would-be candidates who the team tried to recruit. The BBC has not independently verified the NYT's reporting.

In a series of Truth Social posts, Trump too pointed to the report and made a variety of allegations against Peltola, who he argued should be removed from the ballot. He repeated his endorsement for Dan S Sullivan, the incumbent Republican senator, writing: "Dan is a GREAT man, has ALWAYS delivered for Alaska."

Alaska's ranked-choice voting system means that voters could select both Sullivans if they are unsure at the ballot box.

The battle threatens to delay the full picture of nationwide results following the midterm elections. The ultimate question of which party controls Congress will have a significant bearing on the remaining two years of Trump's presidency.

Trump administration sues to block certification of upcoming Alaska election

Alaska's Democratic Senate candidate pauses midterms campaigning after car crash

A statement from an Alaskans for Mary spokesperson, written prior to Dunleavy's call for an investigation, said: "Mary got in this race because Alaskans deserve a champion who is fighting to lower their costs and put Alaska first, and no tweet or threat from any DC politician will keep her away from that fight.

"The Alaskans for Mary campaign has no involvement with either Sullivan campaign."

In a statement given to US media, the DSCC likewise denied that it had been involved in any such scheme.

Peltola earlier this week paused campaigning activities in order to recover after she and her family sustained "minor injuries" in a car crash.

articles.title: Five minutes to doomsday: US and world leaders’ scary talk of looming disaster
articles.summary: Russia’s hybrid war against Europe, the unfinished war in Iran, and increased cyber-attacks all point to potential disaster.
articles.body:
The Doomsday Clock, last adjusted in January, has not since moved any closer to forecasting global catastrophe. But media headlines over the course of 2026 have moved in that direction and are suggestive that midnight is drawing nearer.

Silicon Valley companies, including Anthropic, OpenAI, and xAI, are warning that artificial intelligence — renamed “super intelligence” by President Trump’s executive order — could lead to human extinction if left unchecked. Dario Amodei, the CEO of Anthropic, pegs that risk at 25 percent; Elon Musk at 20 percent.

Even the Pentagon is in doomsday mode. In late September, Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth announced Fortress America , a key element of which is to ensure that major U.S. military bases can continue operating for 90 days or more in the event that civilian power grids, supply chains, and critical infrastructure are disrupted or destroyed.

The undertaking includes building micro nuclear reactors and securing vulnerable networks. Sean Parnell, the Pentagon’s chief spokesman, pointing to the ongoing war in Ukraine, warned that “Power is combat now. Without electricity, you lose communications, assembly lines, and just basic command structures.” He added that we cannot “rely on standard civilian municipal infrastructure to run our national defense.”

Civilian governments are also on guard. Last week, the United Kingdom launched its “Be Ready” campaign , urging citizens to stockpile 72 hours of food, water, cash, medicine, and other essentials.

Russia’s hybrid war against Europe is one factor. Another is the unfinished war in Iran. Another is concern over increased cyber-attacks — including Tehran’s attacks against U.S. water treatment facilities over the last seven months — and the expanding use of AI to wage them.

London is not alone. Ireland issued a “Be Emergency Ready” initiative in August. The Netherlands warned its populace to “Think Ahead” earlier this month. France reminded its citizens this week about its 2025 campaign to prepare a 72-hour survival kit. Japan is introducing a new Disaster Management Agency on November 2.

Even space cannot be considered safe. Earlier this month, according to Under Secretary of State Thomas DiNanno, a Russian military satellite was “exhibiting threatening behavior by intentionally maneuvering dangerously close to a commercial satellite, behaviors consistent with on-orbit weapons operations.”

In response to growing Russian and Chinese operations to “disrupt and degrade U.S. space-enabled capabilities,” Chief of Space Operations Gen. Douglas Schiess announced that “guardians operate on-orbit weapons that can defend the joint force against space-enabled attacks.”

The star wars are upon us. Space is now no longer just about surveillance and command and control, but rather seek and destroy.

On Tuesday, the Defense Intelligence Agency reminded us of this reality in its latest edition of its “ Challenges to Security in Space .” Russia, it warns, “is developing a satellite designed to carry a nuclear weapon despite its obligation to comply with the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, which prohibits the placement of any objects carrying nuclear weapons or any other kinds of weapons of mass destruction into orbit around Earth.”

Yet, as real as these threats are, we should be careful to not let a hybrid reality of still-distant dangers obscure the reality of the immediate perils facing us.

Russia — and Vladimir Putin’s illegal war in Ukraine — are chief among those dangers that arguably equally existential. Doomsday arrives by a different path if Putin is allowed to win or Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and his generals are forced to capitulate. Europe as a whole understands this threat, which is why three out of the Royal Navy’s four Vanguard-class ballistic missile submarines are unusually on patrol at the same time.

The United Kingdom’s submarines carry Trident II D5 missiles that are designed to carry and deliver nuclear warheads.

London, like its European allies, is signaling to the Kremlin in the face of Russia’s hybrid warfare against NATO member-states, that they will not stop militarily and economically supporting Ukraine, or stand idly by while Steve Witkoff or Jared Kushner, acting on behalf of President Trump, attempt to cut business deals with Russia or end sanctions against Putin’s so-called “slush fund. ”

That fund, known as the Russian Direct Investment Fund, is run by Kirill Dmitriev, Putin’s chief negotiating envoy to the U.S. Dmitriev is at the heart of discussions with Witkoff and Kushner to essentially sell out Ukraine in exchange for Russian riches — or, in our view, for the ultimate fool’s gold that Putin will promise but never deliver.

Trump has long railed against Europe for paying for Russia’s war against it by purchasing Russian energy. During an address to the United Nations in 2025, he criticized NATO allies saying, “They’re funding the war against themselves. Who the hell ever heard of that?”

Yet now, alongside Trump’s diesel deal and reports of a potential Alaskan oil deal , the White House is the one aiming to fund Putin’s war against the West. Just as he once accused the Europeans, Trump is now paying to get us to doomsday faster.

Clocks get set back this weekend. Trump would do well to set the Doomsday Clock back an hour as well.

Mark Toth writes on national security and foreign policy. Col. (Ret.) Jonathan Sweet served 30 years as a military intelligence officer and led the U.S. European Command Intelligence Engagement Division from 2012 to 2014. They are the co-founders of INTREP360 and the INTREP360 Intelligence Report on Substack.

articles.title: ELI STEELE: SPLC's ‘Hate Map’ helped banks weaponize and exploit White guilt
articles.summary: Eli Steele argues the Southern Poverty Law Center's "Hate Map" led JPMorgan Chase, Wells Fargo, PNC and TD Bank to debank Christian groups.
articles.body: Editor's note: This op-ed is part of a series by Eli Steele exploring White guilt in America and the West. Steele is the director of the newly released documentary essay, "White Guilt." See the film at WhiteGuiltFilm.com. When I was a student at Claremont McKenna College in the 1990s, Morris Dees, the co-founder of the Southern Poverty Law Center, came to speak. Over the years, I have forgotten what he spoke about, but what I do remember is seeing his gun when he adjusted his sports coat. It was the kind of gun that Clint Eastwood carried in "Dirty Harry," only Dees's was burnished silver, with the deep grooves of a six-shooter. Before the speech, he was billed as the man who took on the Ku Klux Klan, and the gun made the legend real. But to those of us in that room, the gun said something more. It told us that racism was alive and thriving, and that Dees needed that gun as a hedge against an evil that might attack at any moment. Now we have learned that the legend Dees and the SPLC crafted and protected over the years has cost certain Americans their bank accounts. In August 2024, the SPLC published an article that dismissed complaints from several Christian groups about debanking. The SPLC writer, R.G. Cravens, struck an accusatory tone against the Christian legal group Alliance Defending Freedom and said it "perpetuated a false conspiracy theory that claims big government and big corporations are victimizing conservative Christians." SPLC SCANDAL UNDERSCORES HOW THE DEMAND FOR RACISM OUTSTRIPS THE SUPPLY | BOBBY BURACK On Oct. 14, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency released a 47-page report on debanking at the nine largest banks it supervises. Regulators reviewed nearly 100,000 complaints and approximately 420,000 pages of bank records. The report found that four of those banks, JPMorgan Chase, Wells Fargo, PNC and TD Bank, referenced the SPLC while closing accounts or denying loans to conservative and religious customers. The report's details are far more damning than the summary. WePay, a subsidiary of JPMorgan, screened customers against a list of terms that included "MAGA," "America First" and the names of SPLC-designated "hate groups." In July 2021, WePay closed an account that was raising money for a "devout Christian's" legal challenge to anti-discrimination laws. In another case, PNC refused a line of credit to a media company because one owner's foundation "has funded several Christian conservative groups, including several identified as hate groups by the Southern Poverty Law Center." A PNC employee explained, "I think it becomes really difficult to justify aligning ourselves with a company whose owners have built very public personas around opinions very contrary to PNC's beliefs/values." What struck me was that none of these banks checked whether what the SPLC alleged was true. The regulators found that "mere allegations, negative press or negative reviews contributed to some banks declining to serve average Americans, even in the absence of any validation of the underlying facts or concerns." It is hard to be shocked these days, but we must recover that ability. Why would a bank let an advocacy group decide who gets an account, without verification of any sort? It wasn't long before I found the answer in the report: "Fear of being on the wrong side of public opinion led at least one bank to distance itself from certain customer affiliations that could possibly be viewed as partisan." The banks had labeled them a "reputation risk." My father, Shelby Steele, has a better name for it: White guilt. He has spent forty years on this question. To paraphrase him, White guilt is the eternal drive by many Whites, especially those on the left, to prove their innocence of racism, to show over and over that they are not complicit in America's historical racial sins. It is this drive that gives White guilt its transactional nature. In order to be able to buy innocence, someone has to have the innocence to sell. And to sell innocence, you need to possess moral authority when it comes to racial matters. The SPLC earned this moral authority in the deep south when it helped integrate the Alabama state troopers and sued the Klan after violent attacks. But the White guilt machine needs a never-ending supply of hate. If racism begins to fade, then what innocence is there to sell? MOMS GROUP LABELED ‘EXTREMIST’ FLIPS SCRIPT ON SPLC AFTER FEDERAL INDICTMENT: 'SHUT IT DOWN' And the Klan ranks had been thinning for years. By the SPLC's own count, the number of Klan groups fell from 130 in 2016 to 72 a year later. The SPLC’s director of its Intelligence Project said they seemed to be "collapsing." As the Klan shrank, the SPLC knew that it had to manufacture racism, and it did this by widening the definition of what could be counted as hateful and racist. It created the "Hate Map", which put mainstream Christian groups like the Family Research Council and Alliance Defending Freedom alongside the Ku Klux Klan and the Aryan Brotherhood. In 2021, it counted 733 "hate groups." In 2022, it counted 1,225 "hate and antigovernment extremist groups," many of them parents' groups focused on education. Today the list includes Moms for Liberty, PragerU and Turning Point USA. Every bank knew it was the kiss of death to be seen doing business with the Klan. And when these bankers saw the Christian and conservative groups in the same category as the Klan, they took these accusations on faith. They cut off the customers the SPLC named. In return, they got their innocence. Their banks were cleansed of racists. JPMorgan may have been the most savvy of them all. It donated to the SPLC and then its own subsidiary used the SPLC’s labels to close accounts it had flagged as racist. It bought innocence and, simultaneously, used it as a weapon. MIKE DAVIS: SOUTHERN POVERTY LAW CENTER: A TALE OF A RACISM SCAM The power of White guilt is that it leverages the charge of racism mercilessly. It never has to prove the charge — the charge itself is enough. That has been the power of SPLC all along and it is a most lucrative one. The ones who paid were those who were accused of being Christians who hold the same views as millions of Americans. They were put into the race box and charged accordingly. The gun that Morris Dees wore to my college turned out to be theater. We believed that it meant that racism was a living threat that might erupt any day now. Decades later, as I have followed the SPLC’s record, I have come to understand that the "Hate Map" is part of the same theater. The banks believed it because it was cheaper than challenging the methodologies of the SPLC and risking their judgement, the racist charge included. This is the White guilt transaction that my father has long described and warned us against. The gift of this OCC report is that it reveals the truth that many of us have long suspected but could never answer. This report details what happened. But the harder question still remains: what do these banks, the SPLC and everyone who profited from this White guilt machine owe the people that they falsely put on that list? articles.title: Rufián señala a PP y PSOE tras el accidente ferroviario de Urda: “Un fallo humano es el reflejo de un sistema de seguridad fallido”
articles.standfirst: El portavoz de ERC responsabiliza a los recortes en inversión ferroviaria y a la liberalización del mercado
articles.summary: El portavoz de ERC responsabiliza a los recortes en inversión ferroviaria y a la liberalización del mercado
articles.body: Gabriel Rufián se ha pronunciado sobre el accidente ferroviario ocurrido en Urda, Toledo, en el que se vieron implicados dos trenes de alta velocidad, y ha cuestionado que la responsabilidad pueda recaer exclusivamente en un posible error humano. El diputado de Esquerra Republicana de Catalunya ha publicado un mensaje en el que pone el foco en el funcionamiento del sistema ferroviario y en las decisiones políticas que, a su juicio, han contribuido a su situación actual. “Un fallo humano es el reflejo de un sistema de seguridad fallido”, ha escrito Rufián, que considera que la seguridad del transporte ferroviario no puede depender de una única persona cuando están en juego cientos de vidas. Sus palabras llegan en un momento en el que la investigación trata de esclarecer las causas del siniestro y determinar qué factores pudieron influir en el choque. El portavoz de ERC ha dirigido sus críticas tanto al Partido Popular como al PSOE, a los que atribuye responsabilidades políticas por la evolución de la inversión y la gestión del sistema ferroviario. “Una sola persona no puede ser responsable de la vida de centenares en cuanto al transporte ferroviario se refiere”, ha defendido. En su mensaje, Rufián ha señalado que “los únicos nombres y apellidos en todo esto son los recortes en inversión del PP primero y la liberalización salvaje del mercado del PSOE después”. De esta manera, ha vinculado el debate sobre el accidente con las políticas ferroviarias desarrolladas durante los gobiernos de ambos partidos. El diputado también ha cuestionado la gestión de la información relacionada con el siniestro y ha reclamado que se depuren responsabilidades. “Una 'situación inasumible' requiere de asunción de responsabilidades, no de filtraciones para trasladarlas”, ha concluido. Las declaraciones de Rufián se producen mientras continúa la investigación para esclarecer las circunstancias del accidente. Por el momento, las críticas políticas no sustituyen las conclusiones técnicas que deberán determinar qué ocurrió y si existieron fallos en los sistemas de seguridad o en los protocolos de circulación.

"Today’s New York Times reporting reveals disturbing new evidence of an organized effort to manipulate Alaska’s elections by recruiting candidates — including one with the same name as an incumbent U.S. Senator — to deliberately confuse voters and misdirect their votes. The Alaska Division of Elections investigated these very concerns in June of this year. The new reporting substantially supports the Division’s findings," Dunleavy noted in a post on X. MARY PELTOLA'S CAMPAIGN, DEMS BACKED COVERT SCHEME TO FIELD SPOILER CANDIDATES IN ALASKA SENATE RACE: REPORT "I am therefore directing the Department of Public Safety to investigate whether this scheme violated Alaska’s laws and whether criminal charges or civil action are warranted. Sullivan is one of the candidates on the ballot in Alaska's ranked-choice U.S. Senate voting contest, there is another candidate on the same ballot named Daniel J. The group worked to coax other would-be spoilers into the race, to dilute the incumbent’s support and help catapult the Democrat to victory." On Oct. 22, the DOJ filed a federal lawsuit seeking to delay certification if Sen. Dan S. Sullivan loses and votes cast for Daniel J. Sullivan could have changed the result, pending an investigation into whether voters mistakenly selected the wrong candidate. In an interview with Sean Hannity on Wednesday night, Sen. We have a vision for Alaskans that the Alaskan people want, and when they recognize that, they're like, ‘shoot, I guess we got to cheat.’ "What's remarkable here is that even today, she has not apologized. Even today, she's kind of playing as if nothing happened," Sen. Sullivan added. "The Alaskans for Mary campaign has no involvement with either Sullivan campaign and did not recruit any candidates into the race," the Peltola campaign asserted in a statement to the Times.
