articles.title: Leo Terrell takes Trump administration's antisemitism fight nationwide on 15-city tour
articles.summary: Leo Terrell's 15-city "American Tour Against Hate" brings FBI and Justice Department officials directly into Jewish communities facing unaddressed threats.
articles.body: The Justice Department's Antisemitism Task Force Chairman Leo Terrell is taking the Trump administration’s fight against antisemitism directly into Jewish communities on a 15-city nationwide tour, and he says he means business. Terrell told Fox News Digital that local leaders have too often failed to respond while Jewish Americans face threats in their schools, workplaces and houses of worship. "The whole purpose of this tour is to go to where the problem is at, to address their needs, and to provide them with federal support," Terrell said. "Antisemitism is now, and we have to come up with solutions for the future." ANTISEMITIC VIOLENCE REACHES DEADLIEST LEVEL SINCE 1994, NEW GLOBAL REPORT FINDS The "American Tour Against Hate" began Oct. 14 in Michigan, bringing representatives from the Justice Department, FBI and Labor Department together with Jewish residents, students, educators and religious leaders. The federal officials addressed antisemitism in workplaces and schools, as well as the enforcement of hate-crime laws. Terrell said the tour was created to reach communities that feel ignored or abandoned by local officials and to connect them directly with federal resources. "We had the FBI at the first tour meeting because some of these cities have failed to prosecute hate crimes," Terrell said, naming Los Angeles, Boston, San Francisco, New York and Detroit. He did not identify specific unprosecuted cases. Terrell said every stop on the tour would include a public event followed by visits to synagogues, Jewish schools and community centers. WOMAN BUSTED IN NYC RABBI SYRINGE ATTACK ALLEGEDLY STABBED ANOTHER JEWISH MAN HOURS EARLIER: REPORT "The tour is really two days," he said. "We have a two-hour tour event where the community is invited. You know what we do the next day? I spend the next day, all day in the Jewish community." The tour comes as Jews remain disproportionately targeted in religiously motivated hate crimes. According to the latest FBI data, law enforcement agencies reported 1,528 single-bias anti-Jewish hate-crime incidents in 2025. The data also showed that 62.4% of victims of religious-bias hate crimes were targeted because of anti-Jewish bias. Terrell characterized protecting Jewish students and religious communities as a "24-7 obligation," encompassing colleges, K-12 schools and synagogues. He also criticized the financial burden Jewish institutions face to protect students and worshipers, describing security expenses as a "Jewish tax." Universities remain a major focus of Terrell’s work. He warned university presidents that federal scrutiny would continue if Jewish students remained unprotected, saying potential violations would not disappear with a change in administration. JEWISH CAMPUS LIFE AT A ‘CROSSING POINT’ AS STUDENTS WEIGH ANTISEMITISM RISKS, NEW REPORT SHOWS "All these campus presidents are on notice," he said. "You know what I think they’re trying to do? I think they’re trying to wait out President Trump. It’s not gonna happen." He added, "Because if they fail to take care of Jewish American students, all students, we’re going back at them, each school, because those are ongoing violations," he said. "My philosophy is quite simple. Don’t cut deals with these guys," Terrell added. "Force them to go to court, get a court order settlement to make sure they are under the gun to protect Jewish American students." Asked about professors and those allegedly encouraging harassment, Terrell pointed to what he described as overseas influence on campuses. "I think, first of all, there’s a lot of money being brought in from overseas to influence the administration, the faculty members and what I call professional harassers," he said. Asked specifically whether foreign funding and organizational coordination were being investigated, Terrell said, "That is one of the tools." BIPARTISAN DUO LAUNCHES CONGRESSIONAL CAUCUS TO CONFRONT ANTISEMITISM AT COLLEGES "The influence of overseas money as it impacts college campuses and really throughout this country to promote antisemitism. Let me tell you right now, that’s being investigated," he said. His call for broader participation extended to young Christians. Terrell spoke to more than 200 students at the Christian Leaders Summit Forum in Lynchburg, Virginia, hosted by the Combat Antisemitism Movement. Asked why their participation mattered, Terrell called it "probably the most important meeting I’ve ever had in my job," emphasizing the students’ youth and Christian faith. SIGN UP FOR ANTISEMITISM EXPOSED NEWSLETTER "This fight against antisemitism has to include everyone in this country," he said. "Antisemitism is not a Jewish issue. It’s an American issue. It’s a Western civilization issue." "So I need these young people to join me on the stage, telling the Jewish community, telling all Americans we are together in fighting antisemitism," he added. "Religious freedom must be available to all Americans." Asked what Jewish Americans who feel abandoned could count on him to deliver, Terrell urged them to seek help. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "I will never say no," he said. "I will never say no to help. Call my office, call the Department of Justice."

articles.summary: In today’s issue: ▪ Obama hits back in cheesecake battle ▪ Peltola denies recruiting other Sullivan ▪ Bolsonaro arrives in U.S. ▪ Netanyahu accuses Arab parties of fraud Former President Obama kicked his feud with President Trump up a notch on Wednesday as he tries to help the blue wave materialize in next week’s midterms. Campaigning…
articles.body:
▪ Peltola denies recruiting other Sullivan

▪ Netanyahu accuses Arab parties of fraud

Former President Obama kicked his feud with President Trump up a notch on Wednesday as he tries to help the blue wave materialize in next week’s midterms.

Campaigning for Democrats in Georgia, Obama responded to Trump’s comments pushing back on his own remark comparing the president’s White House renovations to the Cheesecake Factory — if it were decorated by the late Iraqi dictator Sadam Hussein .

“They mobilized a whole-of-government response to that joke, not to inflation, but to that joke,” he said. “This is what I mean when I say these are not serious people.”

Obama stirred the pot during another campaign stop in Ohio over the weekend, he poked fun at the White House renovations, which are reportedly expected to cost at least $900 million .

“He’s got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory,” he said.

The former Iraqi dictator’s palaces were famously adorned with gold, which has been a common feature in Trump’s renovations as well. Cheesecake Factories are known for their maximalist, eclectic decor.

Trump fired back on the remark during a Monday rally in Mississippi.

“He said, ‘This isn’t a Cheesecake Factory.’ Can you believe it? Which is a very successful company. He doesn’t like successful companies,” he said.

The White House leaned into Obama’s comments, posting a fake Cheesecake Factory menu touting Trump administration policies in a post on the social platform X. It said the list of Trump’s accomplishments is the “only thing bigger” than the restaurant’s menu.

Various conservative commentators also jumped on the remarks, arguing they showed Obama was out of touch with the average American.

Obama argued Wednesday that Trump seemed more bothered by the comparison to the restaurant chain than his biting criticism of the president’s economic policies.

“Of course, the real problem is the price has gotten so high, a lot of folks can barely afford to go out to eat, so you would think that this administration would be spending time worrying about that. But that was the interesting thing about how the administration responded to the speech I gave,” Obama said.

The exchange is just one front in the closing days of the most expensive midterm battle in history.

Despite the president’s unpopularity and some Republicans distancing from him, Trump and the GOP have pinned their hopes on his ability to turn out the base in red states. And Obama still holds the role as the star-powered closer for Democrats.

The former president has made a few key campaign stops over the past week to rally support for Democrats in tough races. He appeared with Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed in Detroit on Saturday, despite the candidates past critiques of Obama’s policies.

“Well, we’ve lived through two Trump terms now,” El-Sayed told “Meet the Press” host Kristen Welker about his past criticism . “So, look, I know that President Obama was handed a really difficult set of circumstances, and he did his best.”

Obama also joined Democrats Sherrod Brown and Amy Acton as they campaign for Senate and governor, respectively, in Ohio before his Georgia rally for Sen. Jon Ossoff and gubernatorial candidate Keisha Lance Bottoms .

Trump has had campaign stops every day this week in the race’s homestretch. He made his third visit this month to Ohio last night, seeking to boost Sen. Jon Husted (R) and Vivek Ramaswamy .

He zeroed in on the report that Senate Democrats worked with Alaska Senate candidate Mary Peltola ‘s campaign to recruit a spoiler candidate on the ballot. (More on that below.)

“That’s what they’re good at – cheating,” Trump said.

Lots of helpful information for Medicare participants and those in the healthcare space.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth ousted a top military strategist from the Pentagon, the latest senior officer removed from the department under Hegseth’s leadership. The officer fired was Army Lt. Gen. Brett Sylvia, who served as the director for strategy, plans and policy, J-5 on the Joint Staff, two U.S. officials familiar with the situation said.

The Federal Election Commission’s electronic filing system has been restored and is back online following technical issues it experienced just a week before Election Day. What caused the outage is unclear, though Reuters reported that the agency’s website was the target of hacking.

A federal judge has ordered a new hearing on the president’s plans to redevelop East Potomac Park to create a professional-style golf course after Trump vowed to continue with his schedule despite a court order blocking additional construction. The hearing will be held either Friday or Monday.

QUITE CONTRARY: Former Rep. Mary Peltola , the Democratic Senate candidate in Alaska, is denying new reporting from The New York Times suggesting her campaign worked with national Democrats to recruit candidates — including Daniel J. Sullivan — to pull votes from incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska).

“The Alaskans for Mary campaign has no involvement with either Sullivan campaign. Like Mary, our campaign is focused on lowering costs and fixing the rigged system in DC. and did not recruit any candidates into the race,” Peltola’s campaign said in a statement to The Hill.

The Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee (DSCC) also told The Hill it had “no involvement” in recruiting the other Sullivan, who has backed Peltola’s previous statewide campaigns but launched his Senate bid as a Republican before recently switching his party affiliation to “undeclared.”

The Times investigation cites 12 sources and references text messages and documents purporting to show Peltola campaign aides, campaign lawyers and staffers at the DSCC involved in an effort to recruit candidates to siphon off votes.

That practice, known as ballot “stacking,” is generally legal and has been used by both parties in Alaska, where there’s an unusual nonpartisan, top-four voting system.

The Times investigation did not establish criminal wrongdoing, but Trump responded to the reporting yesterday by accusing Democrats of committing perjury and demanding that both Peltola and the “FAKE Dan Sullivan” be removed from the ballot.

The State Department extended visas to Bolsonaro and his family after Brazil’s Supreme Court tried to block Bolsonaro from leaving the country and ordered him to surrender his passports, since the former presidential candidate was under investigation for alleged financial crimes.

Trump said this week that he “would approve” of Bolsonaro coming to the U.S., calling the election “rigged.”

VOTING OPENS : A window is now open for members of the Cornell University Faculty Senate to vote on a motion of no confidence in President Michael Kotlikoff in light of the backlash to the university’s handling of an alleged gang rape of a student in 2024.

The 75-member body will have one week to vote on the motion, which wouldn’t remove Kotlikoff from office but mark a major rebuke of his administration.

Cornell has been facing widespread backlash around the country after a woman identified as Jane Doe filed a lawsuit alleging that seven members of a fraternity had raped her. No criminal charges were pursued against the accused, even as the woman said she reported the incident at the time.

She told the faculty senate in a letter earlier this month that she felt “unsupported and disbelieved” by Kotlikoff, who admitted he didn’t reach out to her after he learned of the alleged assault in 2024.

ELECTION STUNT : Conservative activist James O’Keefe and right-leaning commentator Cam Higby were charged Wednesday over a stunt they pulled during Minnesota’s primaries in August, in which they misrepresented themselves using registered voters’ names at polling places.

Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty announced O’Keefe and Higby are facing felony charges of unlawful voting and identity fraud.

O’Keefe and Higby donned what O’Keefe called “Muslim attire” during the state’s Aug. 11 primaries and spoke in fake accents at Minnesota polling places. They filmed their experience in an attempt to show weaknesses associated with a state law allowing Minnesotans to vouch for people who recently moved to an area if their address can’t be otherwise confirmed .

Moriarty said O’Keefe and Higby didn’t ultimately sign the oath confirming an address or cast a vote. She noted that vouching as a form of confirming eligibility is very rare, only accounting for 0.6 percent of votes cast in 2024.

IT’S THE ECONOMY, STUPID: The final economic picture is taking shape in the last days of the campaign season, which has been dominated by concerns of rising inflation and high costs, especially as the Iran war has driven up oil and gas prices.

The Federal Reserve held interest rates steady yesterday, a month after officials raised rates by a quarter point for the first time in more than three years. But economists and market analysts overwhelmingly expect more rate hikes on the horizon, with CME FedWatch putting chances of a rate hike at December’s meeting at 79.4 percent.

“The committee believes that the accumulation of more information will help it determine the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the 2 percent goal,” Fed Chair Kevin Warsh told reporters.

The latest inflation data offered little relief to Americans. The consumer price index showed prices rose 3.7 percent over the year that ended in September, up from 3.4 percent in August. More than half of that monthly increase was driven by gas prices, which rose 9.1 percent that month.

The Trump administration argues inflation has come down on some non-energy goods, and insists gas prices will drop as soon as the Iran war is finished, which the president has predicted could end right after the midterms.

Voters will get another round of economic data today at 8:30 a.m. EDT, when the Commerce Department releases its first estimate of third-quarter gross domestic product (GDP) and the Fed’s preferred measure of inflation.

Economists surveyed by The Wall Street Journal expect the economy to have grown at a 3.1 percent annual rate, up from 2.2 percent in the second quarter. But they also expect the personal consumption expenditures price index to show prices rising in September from 3.7 percent a year earlier, up from 3.4 percent in August.

POST-ELECTION MORASS : Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his Likud party are accusing Israel’s Arab political parties of fraud in the country’s elections as his bloc appears on track to finish first but fall short of a governing majority.

Netanyahu shared a statement from his party Wednesday, the day after Israel’s first parliamentary elections since the Oct. 7, 2023, attack and the ensuing Gaza war, accusing the two main Arab parties of engaging in bribery, voter intimidation and forgery to influence the election results.

The two parties, the Joint List and Ra’am, had their best performance ever in an Israeli election, likely giving them significant influence as the work begins to form a governing coalition making up a majority of the Knesset’s 120 seats. The Arab parties are currently expected to win as many as 19 seats, based on the latest vote count.

Netanyahu’s bloc is expected to win about 53 seats, more than the opposition bloc, led by former military chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot . But that’s still not enough by itself to form a government.

The Hill’s Laura Kelly reports from Israel that Netanyahu’s fortunes changed Wednesday as his party and its coalition partners edged out Eisenkot’s group, but the prime minister still remains without a clear path to victory. That could leave the Arab parties as the kingmakers unless another deal is reached.

Likud said it is turning over hundreds of witness accounts and pieces of evidence to the Israeli police, the Central Elections Committee and the domestic security service, known as Shin Bet. The party didn’t publicly release evidence of what it collected.

With the election wrapping up, attention will shift to Israeli President Isaac Herzog , who is tasked with picking which party he believes can most likely form a governing coalition based on the results. Even though Likud won more seats than any other party, Herzog doesn’t have to choose it first.

articles.title: The data industry has become a full-blown threat to US national security
articles.summary: Our adversaries don’t need to invent a new intelligence capability to exploit our information. They can already buy it.
articles.body:
This summer, my team bought three months of commercially available data to see what someone — perhaps someone ill-intentioned — could learn about American troops.

We started with a military installation publicly associated with some of our most sensitive special operations units. We pulled the advertising IDs seen there. There were tens of thousands.

We then looked for IDs that also appeared at two other publicly known special operations locations. A few hundred remained. We picked one phone that spent its nights at a house. Public property records and social media led us to an Army officer publicly described as working in logistics. His movements told us something else. Our researchers eventually confirmed that his actual role was one about which an adversary would care a great deal.

A few more clicks led to photos of his children.

The phone was his personal phone. We did not hack it. We did not compromise a government network or do anything illegal. We did not subpoena a wireless carrier. All we had to do was buy commercially available data.

The exercise made me uncomfortable, and rightly so. We were looking at the movements of an American service member and, indirectly, his family. A foreign intelligence service, not operating under our Constitution, can buy much of the same data we bought. So could a private company, a criminal organization or anyone else with access to the market.

When I served as a Green Beret, finding someone through his phone required expensive equipment and capabilities that largely belonged to governments. Today, a laptop and a data set available for purchase by anyone can get you surprisingly close.

AI makes the problem worse. It can sort through enormous datasets and identify patterns that once took an analyst days to piece together. Stanford’s AI Index found that the cost of running capable AI models fell more than 280-fold between late 2022 and late 2024. The economics of surveillance have changed.

U.S. Central Command has reported receiving multiple threat reports involving adversary use of commercial location data to target or surveil U.S. personnel during Operation Epic Fury.

The data can also be remarkably cheap. Duke University researchers purchased data about service members that included home addresses and information about their children for as little as 12 cents per person.

The Pentagon has finally started responding. On Sept. 4, Sen. Ron Wyden (D-Ore.) and Rep. Pat Harrigan (R-N.C.) released responses from the military services showing that the Army, Air Force, Department of the Navy and Special Operations Command had disabled mobile advertising IDs on government-issued phones. That closes a real vulnerability, and the services deserve credit for moving on it.

But that would not have stopped us from finding the officer we found this summer. His government phone wasn’t what exposed him — we found him through the phone in his own pocket, along with public records and information his family had posted online. That distinction matters, because government guidance governing government devices does not eliminate the data generated by personal devices.

Wyden and Harrigan raised the same concern in their September letter, including the possibility that personal phones carried onto military installations remain an important source of commercial location data.

Turning off an advertising ID also does nothing to data that has already been collected. Commercial datasets can preserve years of history. An adversary looking at an officer today may be able to reconstruct where that officer lived, trained, traveled and worked long before the setting was changed.

I am often asked whether a burner phone or a privacy-focused carrier solves this. Both can help, but neither makes the problem disappear.

A burner phone stops being anonymous when you load your normal apps onto it, carry it between your home and office, connect it to familiar Wi-Fi networks, or routinely place it next to the phone everyone already knows belongs to you.

The same problem exists with a phone that has no cellular service at all. Wi-Fi networks, apps, advertising technology and other commercial systems continue to generate information that can help connect a device to a person. The cellular carrier is only one part of the data trail.

Congress has started looking at the larger problem. The House-passed Fiscal Year 2027 National Defense Authorization Act addresses what the government calls ubiquitous technical surveillance. The provision would require the Secretary of Defense to designate an organization responsible for coordinating the identification of surveillance vulnerabilities, along with a department-wide strategy, new training, and a plan for establishing a permanent program of record across the department.

Commercial surveillance doesn’t fit neatly inside the traditional boxes of cybersecurity, intelligence, communications or force protection. Different organizations own pieces of the problem. Nobody owns all of it. That makes one-off fixes almost inevitable.

Turn off one identifier and another source of data becomes useful. Remove a record from one broker and it can reappear somewhere else. Lock down a government device and the personal phone beside it may still be broadcasting enough information to identify its owner.

The Department needs an accountable owner responsible for understanding that exposure as a whole: identifying which service members and families are most exposed, assessing what information about them is already commercially available, determining what can be removed or mitigated, and giving commanders a way to understand a person’s digital exposure before deployment and as it changes over time.

The services have already shown that they can move quickly when a vulnerability is clear. Turning off advertising IDs was a useful step.

The harder problem is everything that remains outside that setting: years of existing data, personal phones, apps, public records, social media and an industry built to connect all of it. Our adversaries don’t need to invent a new intelligence capability to exploit that information. They can buy it.

Erik Wittreich is chief executive officer at Veilant and a former Army Green Beret.

articles.title: Judge rejects DOJ request to block California from immediately counting ballots linked to alleged noncitizens
articles.summary: A federal judge blocked the Justice Department from barring California's count of mail ballots from over 20,000 alleged noncitizen voters on its rolls.
articles.body: A federal judge rejected the Justice Department’s request for a temporary restraining order that would have barred California from counting mail ballots from more than 20,000 alleged noncitizen voters, saying the election "is already underway." U.S. District Judge David Carter, in a ruling issued late Wednesday night after a hearing in Los Angeles, said the government's request "would wreak havoc and disrupt the election that is already underway, create a chilling effect on election workers and voters alike, and discount the votes of United States citizens." The Justice Department immediately appealed the decision to the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals. CALIFORNIA MUST RESPOND TO DOJ'S EMERGENCY REQUEST OVER BALLOTS MAILED TO ALLEGED NONCITIZENS, COURT RULES "The district court denied our emergency request to sequester ballots from 20,000 suspected noncitizens," U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli wrote on X. "Every day, more ballots are processed by election officials. This ongoing emergency disenfranchises American citizens through dilution. The Solicitor General authorized an immediate appeal. We filed our Notice of Appeal and will immediately seek an emergency order from the Ninth Circuit." NEWSOM SPARS WITH TRUMP-APPOINTED PROSECUTOR OVER 20,000 SUSPECTED NONCITIZENS ON VOTER ROLLS California mails ballots to all 23 million of its registered voters. More than 3.7 million people have already voted in the state, including more than 500,000 ballots already processed this week with the ballot already out of the envelope, according to court filings. It would be impossible to know which ballot belonged to a particular voter now, according to Los Angeles County officials. BLANCHE WON'T RULE OUT DOJ BLOCKING ELECTION CERTIFICATION IN 'DOOMSDAY' SCENARIO "Eroded trust in our democracy is irreparable," Judge Carter, appointed by former President Bill Clinton, wrote. "Once a vote is segregated, lasting harm has occurred. If the Executive can discount votes and threaten an ongoing election due to unproven allegations, then our democracy is in danger. This Court declines to be a party to such process." STATE DEPARTMENT CONSIDERS SHARING PASSPORT RECORDS FOR VOTER CITIZENSHIP CHECKS Carter said that "states have control over their elections," but the federal government claims it has evidence the state refuses to accept that there are 20,000 noncitizens registered to vote in the state of California. President Donald Trump has repeatedly insisted that states are not doing enough to stop noncitizens from voting, which he says is widespread. Carter said the Justice Department never explained why counting ballots would impair any prosecutions under the law, and California said the DOJ's assertions relied on "suspect data." JUSTICE DEPARTMENT CHARGES 16 ACROSS MULTIPLE STATES WITH ALLEGED ILLEGAL VOTING, ELECTION CRIMES "There are no mysterious databases; this was laid out in publicly filed declarations," Essayli wrote Wednesday night on X. "Voter rolls were compared to USCIS immigration, Social Security, and passport records. We are not changing the rules mid-election, we are enforcing them. It’s unlawful for noncitizens to vote." Registered voters can self-declare to be noncitizens to get removed from the voter roll, and do so while they are seeking naturalization or saying they are ineligible for jury duty. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP In Washington state, the Justice Department on Monday sent a letter asking officials not to count any ballots received from 400 voters it claims are not citizens. Washington had 5 million registered voters as of 2024, state records show. The Associated Press and Reuters contributed to this report.

articles.body:
Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy (R) on Wednesday evening ordered an investigation into whether Mary Peltola’s (D) Senate campaign violated the state law when it reportedly recruited candidates in an effort to detract support from her opponent.

The GOP governor cited The New York Times’s reporting earlier that day that found the Democrat’s campaign was involved in a secret effort to bring on a spoiler candidate with the same name as Sen. Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska) to run in the race.

The efforts were successful, and a retired teacher named Dan J. Sullivan ultimately entered the race. Both Sullivans will appear as options for voters next week under the state’s unusual four-person ballot.

Both Peltola’s campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee denied any involvement in the reported scheme.

Dunleavy wrote in a social media post that the Times’s report revealed new details about an effort to “deliberately confuse voters and misdirect their votes.”

“Alaskans have a fundamental right to vote for the candidate they actually intend to support,” he wrote. “Deliberately tricking voters into casting their ballots for someone else strikes at the integrity of our elections.”

The governor added he was directing the Alaska Department of Public Safety to investigate whether the scheme violated state laws and whether criminal charges or civil action was warranted.

President Trump called for both Peltola and the spoiler candidate to be removed from the ballot and prosecuted on Wednesday.

“The Democrats cheated! They found a man named Dan Sullivan, put him on the Ballot, then lied to the Court, and said they didn’t know anything about it,” he wrote on Truth Social. “That’s perjury. She shouldn’t be allowed to run, and neither should the FAKE Dan Sullivan!”

Last week, the president directed his Justice Department to file a lawsuit calling for the certification of Alaska’s Senate election to be blocked if the incumbent Sullivan lost the race. The suit alleges that Dan J. Sullivan entered the race as a Republican “with the intention of misleading” voters.

articles.title: On the Ballot: The 5 key money moves in the priciest midterms yet
articles.summary: With less than a week left in the most expensive midterms ever, the pressure is on for this cycle’s big spending to pay off. More than $11 billion has poured into races across the country, smashing records as Republicans scramble to keep their House and Senate majorities against a national map that’s shifted in Democrats’…
articles.body:
With less than a week left in the most expensive midterms ever, the pressure is on for this cycle’s big spending to pay off.

More than $11 billion has poured into races across the country, smashing records as Republicans scramble to keep their House and Senate majorities against a national map that’s shifted in Democrats’ favor.

The battleground Senate races in Ohio and Texas have each seen more than $500 million in ad spending, according to the ad-tracking firm AdImpact, as Democrats put Republicans on defense in red territory.

As Democrats fight for a blue wave in the House, eight races from this midterm cycle have already entered the top-10 most expensive on record, according to AdImpact — and gubernatorial race ad spending has hit a record $2.4 billion, up by more than half a billion from the 2022 midterm cycle.

Meanwhile, tech mogul Elon Musk and key super PACs, from crypto groups to AIPAC, are pumping money into races to tip the scales in the closing days.

Here are some of the biggest takeaways from the most expensive midterms on record:

The 2025-26 cycle crossed the threshold this week to become the most expensive cycle ever — surpassing not just past midterms, but past presidential cycles.

According to data tracked by AdImpact , this cycle has seen $11.21 billion in ad spending and reservations as of Monday, edging past the $11.2 billion spent during the 2023-24 presidential cycle.

That staggering dollar figure comes from record-breaking spending on the House, Senate and governor’s races, plus a huge sum from down ballot and state Legislative contests.

Roughly $2.3 billion has been spent on House races, up from $1.6 billion in 2022 and $1.7 billion in 2024, according to AdImpact , as Democrats grow bullish about taking the lower chamber majority.

Spending on governor’s races have also surged to $2.6 billion, up from $1.9 billion in 2022 and just half a billion in 2024. A whopping $3.2 billion has been spent so far on Senate races, up from $2.3 billion in the 2022 midterms and rivaling the $3.2 billion spent on presidential campaigns in 2024.

The chart-smashing numbers signal the intensity of this year’s races as Republicans scramble to keep their hold on Washington through the end of Trump’s second term.

According to recent Federal Election Commission filings, the president’s MAGA Inc. super PAC has spent $277 million over the last six weeks. And the Republican National Committee moved $44 million into its House and Senate campaign arms between mid-August and mid-October in a last-minute fundraising surge.

With less than a week to go before votes are tallied, Decision Desk HQ’s (DDHQ) forecast gives Democrats an 80 percent chance of winning the House — and a probability of just under 60 percent that they flip the Senate.

The Senate races in Texas and Ohio are a coin-toss heading into Election Day, and eye-popping expenses underscore just how desperate both parties are to influence where it falls.

Roughly $558 million had been spent in the Lone Star State as of AdImpact’s Tuesday analysis, and another $500 million had poured into ruby-red Ohio.

The governor’s race in California, where Democrat Xavier Becerra is poised to replace Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) as leader of the state with the highest population and biggest economy in the country, and the Michigan Senate race, where Democrat Abdul El-Sayed is fighting Republican Mike Rogers for the battleground seat, both made the top-10 most expensive non-presidential races on record. Just under $350 million has been spent on each.

It’s the first cycle in which multiple non-presidential races have crossed the $500 million-mark, according to the data.

In Texas, Democrat James Talarico raked in $64 million in the third quarter — more than any Senate candidate ever in that timeframe, his campaign said — compared to $18 million raised in the same period by rival Republican Ken Paxton as the Democrat narrowly leads in recent polls of the GOP-dominated state.

But Republicans and their supporters weren’t backing down in the home stretch: tech mogul Elon Musk poured $158 million into a key super PAC backing Paxton, according to filings ahead of the election, prompting Talarico to accuse Musk of trying to “buy his own personal U.S. senator.”

In Ohio, Democrat former Sen. Sherrod Brown raised $23.1 million to Republican incumbent Sen. Jon Husted’s $5 million in the third quarter.

The GOP-aligned Senate Leadership Fund, the Trump-backed MAGA Inc. and Musk’s America PAC have all poured in for a reported total of $113.5 million attacking Brown, according to the Ohio Capital Journal, compared to $69.5 million in outside groups spending to attack Husted.

Musk announced plans last spring to step back from political spending after injecting hundreds of millions into the 2024 election to boost Trump and Republicans to win their trifecta control of Washington.

Less than a year later, the world’s richest person reversed course, and he’s again become a major player in this year’s pricey midterms.

Musk, whose net worth is just under a trillion dollars, has spent more than $442 million on the midterms, according to his super PAC’s last filing before Election Day, topping the estimated $290 million he spent on 2024 contests.

He’s spent big against Talarico in Texas, including $158 million to the Senate Leadership Fund that was later dispersed to a pro-Paxton super PAC.

Talarico has accused Musk of trying to “buy his own personal U.S. senator,” saying there’s “something deeply wrong” with a political system that allows it to happen.

Of the $11 billion that’s flooded this cycle, just 40 of the biggest donors gave $2.5 billion through mid-October, according to analysis from the Brennan Center. That’s up substantially from $755 million given by the top-40 donors in the 2018 midterms, and $1.2 billion given in the 2022 cycle.

And those top-40 donors have overwhelmingly backed Republicans each cycle since 2018, according to the Brennan Center, with $1.5 billion from GOP donors against less than half a billion from Democrats, and another half a billion from bipartisan sources.

As the top-40 biggest spenders shift further toward the GOP, cryptocurrency has surged as the leading special-interest sector, according to the Brennan Center’s analysis.

Crypto, which was not represented in the top 40 donors before the 2022 elections has now outpaced labor as a leading bipartisan interest.

The crypto industry has spent roughly $176 million across more than a hundred races in a push to elect candidates they expect will be legislative allies, Reuters reported this week.

Fairshake, a major crypto super PAC, has spent millions to back more than a dozen Democrats and Republicans running for the House, The Hill reported earlier this month , including $1 million each on six candidates: Reps. Janelle Bynum (D-Ore.), Steven Horsford (D-Nev.), Derek Tran (D-Calif.), French Hill (R-Ark.), Bill Huizenga (R-Mich.) and Bryan Steil (R-Wis.).

The super PAC also planned to spend at least $30 million in Ohio alone to oppose Brown’s Senate comeback bid, after the crypto industry spent heavily to oust Brown in the 2024 election.

8 House races join all-time top-10 priciest

Democrats are working in overdrive to claw back control of the House this fall, and the spending numbers underscore which close races to watch on Election Day.

Eight House general elections from this midterm cycle have now entered the 10 most expensive on record, according to AdImpact’s Tuesday numbers.

In first place is the race for North Carolina’s 1st Congressional District, where Republican Laurie Buckhout is challenging incumbent Democratic Rep. Don Davis in a 2024 rematch after redistricting made the moderate Davis a top target for the GOP.

Roughly $30 million has been spent on the Democratic side, according to AdImpact, compared to $23 million on the GOP side.

Republicans and Democrats have spent roughly $25 million each in Florida’s 25th Congressional District, where Rep. Jared Moskowitz (D) is running for the redistricted seat against former Boca Raton Mayor Scott Singer (R).

DDHQ rates both races as “lean Democrat,” while Cook Political Report still considers them toss-ups.

In New York’s purple 17th Congressional District, roughly $47 million has been spent in total as Rep. Mike Lawler (R-N.Y.) fights for another term against Democrat Cait Conley.

Around $44 million total has been spent in Michigan’s 10th Congressional District, where Trump-backed Army Capt. Michael Bouchard faces Democrat former special victims prosecutor Christina Hines in a wide-open race. Another $42 million has gone into Texas’s 34th Congressional District, where Rep. Vicente Gonzalez (D-Texas) tries for reelection against Republican Eric Flores after redistricting made his seat redder.

Wisconsin’s 3rd Congressional District, where Republican Rep. Derrick Van Orden and Democrat Rebecca Cooke are in a battleground rematch, and Colorado’s 8th Congressional District, where Democrat Manny Rutinel aims to oust incumbent Rep. Gabe Evans (R-Colo.), also made the all-time top-10, according to AdImpact — with around $42 million and $41 million spent in those districts, respectively.

Voters will decide next week which of this cycle’s pricey campaigns were worth the cost.

Welcome to The Hill’s On The Ballot. We’re Julia Mueller and Caroline Vakil — reach out to us on X ( @jmthewriter + @CarolineVakil) or via email ( jmueller@thehill.com + cvakil@thehill.com.)

The House and Senate forecasts less than a week out from Election Day

Democrats have a 4 in 5 shot of flipping the House and rising odds of taking the Senate with just five days to go before midterm results roll in, according to the latest forecasts from The Hill’s partners at Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ).

The party’s 80 percent probability in the House and 58 percent chance the Senate are their highest marks for either chamber this cycle.

Democrats emerged battered and bruised from the 2024 presidential election, but a string of off-year wins emboldened the party through 2025. Now, the polls point to a real possibility of a blue wave when ballots are tallied on Tuesday.

Republicans, already up against the longtime trend of a president’s party losing ground in a midterm year, have been pummeled by voter frustration with President Trump and the GOP’s handling of the economy, the war in Iran, immigration and more.

As of Wednesday afternoon, Democrats are on track to win 238 seats in the House, according to DDHQ — a 41-seat advantage over Republicans.

The Senate is more of a challenge, but Democrats are narrowly favored to win a 51-seat edge in the upper chamber.

Democrats are also favored in 22 of three-dozen governor’s races on Tuesday’s ballot, on track to flip five offices while Republicans are favored to flip one.

The fight for Control of Congress is expected to come down to a handful of toss-up contests. DDHQ’s latest analysis shows 10 battlegrounds in the House, including dead-head races in Colorado’s 3rd Congressional District, Florida’s 22nd Congressional District, New York’s 17th Congressional District and Pennsylvania’s 8th Congressional District.

There are just 4 toss-up contests in the Senate, according to DDHQ, with marquee showdowns to watch in Iowa, Ohio, Maine and Texas.

articles.title: Bolsonaro declares himself 'leader' of Brazil after fleeing country, arriving in Miami
articles.summary: Brazilian Sen. Flávio Bolsonaro fled to Florida through Argentina after a Supreme Court justice ordered his passport seizure minutes after Lula won.
articles.body: Sen. Flávio Bolsonaro, who lost Brazil's presidential election to leftist incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva on Sunday, declared himself the country's leader after arriving in Florida on Wednesday. Bolsonaro fled his country after Brazilian Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes ordered his passports to be seized less than a day after Lula won the election. "I want to say, not only to my 60 million voters but to the Brazilian people, that I am the leader and that the criminals who stole Brazil’s election are part of a criminal organization that has established a tyranny," he said in an open letter posted on X. According to Reuters, Bolsonaro initially declared himself "the elected president" in a since-deleted post. He then sent out an updated letter on X, which included calling himself the rightful "leader" of Brazil. Bolsonaro, who lost the runoff election by a 3.58% margin, was served with an order to forfeit his passports and not to leave the country on Monday. "I was ordered right on the street to hand over my passports, and I'm also prohibited from leaving the country," Bolsonaro said, according to a Fox News Digital translation of a video he posted to his social media channels Monday. The order was signed by de Moraes, who Bolsonaro supporters accuse of being a staunch ally of Lula. TRUMP'S FINGERPRINTS SEEN ON LATIN AMERICA'S RIGHTWARD SHIFT AS BRAZIL BECOMES NEXT TEST Bolsonaro landed at Opa Locka Executive Airport just north of Miami with his family Wednesday morning after President Donald Trump granted Bolsonaro and his family visas. When asked Wednesday if he would approve of Bolsonaro coming to the U.S. following his defeat, Trump told reporters he would, adding, "I think they’re fine people." "The election ‌was very strange," Trump continued. "And I thought ⁠it was terrible. It’s gotten bad reviews. You look at what happened to their market." BRAZIL’S RAPID ELECTION COUNT PUTS SPOTLIGHT ON VOTING SECURITY AHEAD OF US MIDTERMS Brazil's stock market plummeted Monday after Lula's victory. Its benchmark index, the Ibovespa, closed down nearly 14% on the first day of post-election trading. The Brazilian real also suffered one of its steepest drops in history, losing nearly 11% of its value relative to the U.S. dollar. Trump also said, "I didn’t take ​sides, but it looked like another rigged election." Brazilian news outlet MD+ reported that Brazilian Federal Police requested Bolsonaro's passport seizure order just seven minutes after Brazil's Superior Electoral Court confirmed Lula's victory. Bolsonaro, the son of former Brazilian president Jair Bolsonaro, initially said he would comply with the order, but ultimately chose to leave. THE UNLIKELY SOUTH AMERICAN ALLY HELPING LEAD TRUMP'S DRUG CARTEL CRACKDOWN "I have never thought ‌about leaving the country," Bolsonaro said in a social media video on Monday. "I will hand over my passports and defend myself against this travesty, which is a clear attempt to intimidate me." But Bolsonaro ultimately crossed the border into Argentina, Argentina's National Directorate of Migrations confirmed, saying the Bolsonaro family entered the country "with valid travel documentation and without any legal impediment" Tuesday night. The family then crossed into Ecuador where they boarded a private plane for Florida, according to Time Magazine. Lula called his decision to leave "a shameful act," recalling his own 2018 arrest for corruption. Bolsonaro said the order came as a result of a social media post his brother Eduardo made in which he said Flávio should leave the country if he loses the election. US TAXPAYER DOLLARS ALLEGEDLY FUELED LEFT-WING POLITICAL CAUSES IN LATIN AMERICA Flávio was under multiple criminal investigations for alleged money laundering, corruption and tax evasion, according to Brazilian newspaper Folha de São Paulo. According to Reuters, Bolsonaro denied fleeing Brazil, saying he left to protect himself and his family. He said he was avoiding a witch hunt being carried out by Lula and the Brazilian Supreme Court. "I want to make this clear: I did not flee Brazil," Bolsonaro said. "I left Brazil, but I did not abandon the Brazilian people." On Tuesday, Brazil's Supreme Court also ordered the Federal Police to open an investigation into alleged illegal foreign funding for Bolsonaro’s presidential campaign, specifically focusing on Rockbridge Network, a conservative donor group co-founded by U.S. Vice President JD Vance. articles.title: Tim Scott calls for DOJ investigation of Peltola campaign
articles.summary: Sen. Tim Scott (R-S.C.) on Wednesday called on the Department of Justice (DOJ) to investigate Democrat Mary Peltola’s campaign over reports that the team sought to recruit “spoiler” candidates in Alaska to affect next week’s election. “There’s no doubt that Mary Peltola has been, at least her campaign and the Democrat apparatus, they are involved…
articles.body:
Sen. Tim Scott (R-S.C.) on Wednesday called on the Department of Justice (DOJ) to investigate Democrat Mary Peltola’s campaign over reports that the team sought to recruit “spoiler” candidates in Alaska to affect next week’s election.

“There’s no doubt that Mary Peltola has been, at least her campaign and the Democrat apparatus, they are involved in collusion,” Scott told NewsNation’s Katie Pavlich. “They’ve been colluding together in a coordinated effort to deceive the voters.”

Scott added that, in his opinion, the effort amounts to “a criminal offense.”

“And I’m hoping that the DOJ will take a serious look at all of the evidence that leads in that direction,” he continued. “And factually speaking, when you have the receipt, so to speak, it leads you somewhere. I hope that the DOJ takes all the time necessary to prosecute and investigate this situation.

The South Carolina Republican accused Democrats of “deceiving voters, pretending to be what they’re not” in order to win races, mentioning Texas Senate candidate James Talarico (D) and South Carolina Senate candidate Annie Andrews (D) by name as examples.

“But now, as a candidate on TV, you would think that she’s something else,” Scott said. “And so having the facts are really important. But in Alaska, that’s criminal. And I think that there should be a serious investigation into that.”

The New York Times reported Wednesday that Peltola campaign aides and lawyers, along with Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee (DSCC) staffers, were involved in pushing other candidates, including Alaska Senate candidate Daniel J. Sullivan.

The campaign and DSCC have denied being involved with the reported effort.

Scott’s comments follow President Trump’s claim that Peltola’s campaign perpetuated “such a terrible scheme” and should be barred from running, making the unfounded claim that it was “ELECTION FRAUD.” Trump pointed to Daniel J. Sullivan’s name being on the ballot alongside incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan (R) and said the Democrats should face prosecution.

Last week, the DOJ filed a lawsuit against Alaska over the two Sullivans’ names being on the ballot and claimed presence of a candidate with the same name as the sitting lawmaker would give Peltola an unfair advantage.

Peltola on Sunday asked a federal judge to dismiss the lawsuit, with her lawyers telling Reuters that the complaint was “wholly baseless.”

Attorney General Todd Blanche has said the DOJ’s lawsuit intends to ensure that when ballots are cast, Alaska election officials “have the information necessary to make a determination as to whether Alaskan voters were confused or mislead.”

Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy (R) announced late Wednesday the state would open a probe into the controversy, and whether the alleged recruitment efforts violate state law.

The race is among the most contested of this election cycle as Republicans fight to maintain their control of Congress. The Cook Political Report rates the race as a toss-up, with The Hill’s election partner Decision Desk HQ forecasting a 61-percent probability that Peltola wins.

With less than a week out until Election Day , candidates attempt to leave their final mark on voters.

President Trump will hold a lunchtime rally Thursday in Rock Hill, S.C., on the North Carolina border, to gin up voter enthusiasm for Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.), who is facing a tougher-than-expected race against Democratic opponent Annie Andrews.

He’ll continue GOP efforts to boost Ken Paxton, the state’s attorney general, in his Senate race against Democrat James Talarico. Trump visited Texas three times in October to stump for Paxton in a contest that is also tighter than anticipated.

Former Vice President Harris will be in Macon, Ga., to garner support for Sen. Jon Ossoff (D) in his bid for reelection. Her visit comes one day after former President Obama campaigned on the senator’s behalf in Atlanta.

Obama hammered home Democrats’ affordability message — and also swung back at President Trump in the pair’s Cheesecake Factory spat . “They mobilized a whole of government response to that joke. Not to inflation, but to that joke,” he said.

Mike Dunleavy (R) late Wednesday ordered an investigation into whether Mary Peltola’s (D) Senate campaign violated the state law when it reportedly recruited candidates in an effort to detract support from her Republican opponent. The controversy surrounding Peltola may not change the race much, though.

articles.title: Fox News Power Rankings: South Carolina moves to toss-up
articles.summary: South Carolina's Senate race moves to toss-up as new polling shows Graham tied at 48%, and Trump heads to the Upstate to boost the GOP senator.
articles.body: Updated October 29: We’re updating this forecast to move South Carolina from Lean R to Toss-up. As this week’s Power Rankings reported, Republicans already viewed this as an uncomfortably close race. That belief is now widely shared. Tonight, the president is headed back there to help Sen. Darline Graham in the Upstate, where she underperformed in her primary runoff against Rep. Ralph Norman. New polling has Democratic challenger Annie Andrews and Graham tied at 48%-48%. The Senate is still a toss-up with six states to decide the majority. On a good night for the Democrats, their ceiling rises to 54 seats. A good night for the Republicans could see them retain control with up to 52 seats. — It seems like there are two electorates in these midterms. The first is frustrated with President Trump and ready to reject Republicans. It includes growing numbers of independent, rural, and Hispanic voters who say they’ll vote for a Democrat. That’s what the latest round of House polling shows, including a survey last week that had Democrats up 11 points on the generic ballot, and Fox’s most recent national poll. FOX NEWS POWER RANKINGS: TRUMP COUNTRY AT A CROSSROADS The second electorate is wavering on Republicans but won’t necessarily hand Democrats the Senate. These are the voters in the Midwest and a few other places. They say they prefer the Democrat or Republican in their states by a point or two at most. That’s the right conclusion from most of the battleground Senate polling. How could both things be true? In other words, if Democrats have such a wide lead in the House, won’t the Senate fall too? Both are true, and a big lead in the House doesn’t necessarily translate to the Senate. These voters are all in the same electorate, and they only seem divorced from each other because the House and Senate maps are so far apart this year. TRUMP-BACKED SENATOR ADMITS GOP FACES NIGHTMARE SCENARIO IN STATE REPUBLICANS HAVEN'T LOST IN 90 YEARS The president’s declining approval rating and Democratic advantages on the issues will likely deliver them the House, and possibly by many seats. Those advantages have also allowed the blue team to play in a lot of Senate races that Republicans thought were unreachable, but only to the point of making them battlegrounds. The road to a Senate majority goes through several states that Trump won by 11 points or more. Democrats can win any of these races. If Republicans turn out and stay loyal to their party, the climb for the left will be steep. That’s why the Senate is a toss-up. Voters could give Democrats a majority, and maybe with several seats to spare. They could also let the Republicans keep control. We’ll find out in seven days. Democrats have strong advantages on most key issues In his 11-year political career, President Trump has triumphed over almost all of the threats to his power. The exception was the coronavirus pandemic, which was the top issue for voters in the 2020 election and ushered in the Biden presidency. It was also one of the few threats that Trump has faced from abroad. This time, Trump and the Republicans face a new foreign opponent: Iran. The administration’s decision to start joint U.S.-Israeli military strikes against the nation in February has cast a shadow over the GOP. TRUMP WON THIS RELIABLY RED STATE BY DOUBLE DIGITS. NOW A DEADLOCKED RACE IS BRINGING HIM BACK First, it has impacted Trump’s approval rating, which will decide the fate of many congressional Republicans and has fallen since the war began. It was 44% in the last pre-war survey and sits at 36% now. The war has also given Democrats advantages on the top issues. In Fox’s October survey, Iran played a role in four issues that more than two-thirds of voters said they were concerned about: inflation (85%), gas prices (83%), government leadership (79%), and the war in Iran itself (75%). Most voters said they preferred the Democrats to handle those issues: 16 points on inflation, 12 points on gas prices, 11 points on leadership, and 9 points on foreign policy. Republicans are competitive on home turf Still, voters are not convinced that the Senate should change hands. That comes down to the territory. Trump won seven of these ten battleground states in 2024, and six of them by double digits. That includes Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Ohio, South Carolina, and Texas. Democrats don’t need to win all of those states to take the Senate, but it’s hard to see how they get to 51 seats without at least two of them. While former Democratic Senator Sherrod Brown leads in Ohio, the other states are close. Turnout, a polling error in either direction, or both could decide them. There’s also a lot of undecided vote. In Alaska, Iowa, and Kansas, three states with recent high-quality polling, an average of 10% of voters say they haven’t decided who they will support or won’t support the major candidates. Any guess on how those voters will break at the ballot box is only a guess. All we know from prior results is that the overall electorate leans conservative, so the Democrats have the tougher assignment to bring them over to their side (or keep them at home). There are far fewer undecided voters in Texas, where last week’s Fox News Poll showed a tied race at 49%-49%. If Democrats only win two Trump-won battlegrounds, they’ll need to win three other races where former Vice President Harris delivered single-digit victories in 2024: Maine, Minnesota, and New Hampshire. Democrats are ahead in the latter two. Maine could go either way. While Democrats win its presidential races, it could just as easily be considered a Republican state when Susan Collins is on the ballot. The final Fox News Power Rankings for 2026 feature three shifts in the Senate and nineteen in the House. A tight gubernatorial race is also on the move. Senate: Democrats are favored in 48 seats; Ohio moves to Lean D and South Carolina moves to Toss-up Both parties are short of a majority in this forecast. Democrats are favored in 48 seats and Republicans are ahead in 46 (they would control the Senate with 50 seats because the Vice President breaks ties). On a good night for Democrats, the party would win most or all the toss-ups, taking the majority with up to 54 seats. In that scenario, other competitive states would also come into focus, including one rated Lean R, and on a great Democratic night, two more rated Likely R. A good night for the Republicans would see them simply hold on to most of the states they already have, up to a ceiling of 52 seats. The party also has opportunities to flip a couple of states, including Minnesota and New Hampshire. Three states are moving in this forecast. Ohio In Ohio, Brown has enjoyed a lead in three Fox News polls this year, including last week’s survey, which had him five points ahead of Republican incumbent Sen. Jon Husted at 52%-47%. Ohio voters are very familiar with Brown, having sent him to the Senate three times. That has made it hard for Husted to campaign on socialism and woke politics, themes that Republicans elsewhere see as their strongest cards to play. Ohio moves from Toss-up to Lean D. ("Lean D" means the Democrat has an edge but it’s still a highly competitive race. We define every ranking and the process for setting them on FoxNews.com.) South Carolina As this week’s Power Rankings previously reported , Republicans already viewed this as an uncomfortably close race. That belief is now widely shared. Tonight, the President is headed back there to help Senator Graham in the Upstate, where she underperformed in her primary runoff against Rep. Ralph Norman. South Carolina moves from Lean R to Toss-up. Mississippi Mississippi is a Republican stronghold, but Trump’s decision to rally there over other deep red states is a sign that the party thinks it’s competitive. GOP Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith faces Democratic District Attorney Scott Colom in a race where protein choice has become a breakout issue. Mississippi moves from Solid R to Likely R. House: The floor for Democrats ticks up four seats to 223 Democrats are still likely to flip the House this November, and in this forecast, they’re predicted to take at least 223 seats. Since a good night for the Democrats would see them take most of the toss-up races, they could end up with as many as 240 seats. (On a great Democratic night, the party would pick up most of the Lean R districts as well, taking them as high as 252 seats.) Republicans have 195 seats in their columns. A good night for them would take that total up to around 212. That’s six short of a majority, but enough to make life difficult for the next Democratic House Speaker, who would have to balance the demands of the moderate and far-left wings of the party. Nineteen more races have shifted in the Democrats’ direction this week, all on the same themes outlined in the last House update: national and district polling, top-of-the-ticket strength, and rural voter erosion. The earliest-closing districts on election night will give some sense of the House’s future. Keep an eye on Kentucky’s 6th district, which covers Lexington and a large central area of the state. Trump won here by 15 points in the last presidential election. Thanks to a combination of left-leaning college voters and farmers grappling with higher costs, it looks close this cycle. The district moves from Lean R to Toss-up. Governor: Ad or no ad, the Ohio governor’s race moves to Lean D Finally, Ohio’s gubernatorial race is also on the move. The campaign between Democrat Amy Acton and Republican Vivek Ramaswamy was the top story in politics last week after Ramaswamy ran an ad featuring Acton’s mother, who called her daughter a liar. Acton has been estranged from her mother since age 12, when she says she and her brother left her family home because her mother’s husband was sexually abusing her. Acton’s brother now appears in a response ad discussing their family history. This ratings change is less about the response to the ad (Ramaswamy and President Trump are supportive of the commercial; most others including Husted and Governor Mike DeWine are against it) than it is about the fact that the Ramaswamy campaign felt the need to run it. While Ramaswamy sat only two points behind Acton in last week’s Fox poll, he’s an average of seven points behind in other high-quality polls since September. The businessman and onetime presidential hopeful has struggled in favorability ratings throughout his political career. This ad is unlikely to help. The Ohio governor’s race moves from Toss-up to Lean D. — CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Fox News’ special coverage of the 2026 midterm elections begins at 6pm ET next Tuesday, November 3, anchored by Bret Baier and Martha MacCallum.
